This research introduces a novel application of federated learning in the field of digital pathology, specifically for the automated detection of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. The project combines the advantages of centralized deep learning approaches with the benefits of working with entire image collections at decentralized institutions. Through a demonstration on a large, multi-institutional dataset consisting of 4,000 whole-slide images from four leading cancer research centers, this study showcases the first successful implementation of this technique in digital pathology. The results reveal that federated learning yields comparable outcomes to a centralized approach and significantly reduces computational expenses by eliminating the need for data transfer. The research culminates in a robust, institutionally-specific model for each of the participating institutions, as well as a comprehensive central model, all made publicly available for the benefit of the scientific community. The source code and training data can be accessed at https://github.com/constantinmej/fuladil. The federated learning framework has the potential to accelerate and standardize the development of AI-powered tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte detection across the cancer research community. With continued advancements, this technique could be applied to other domains within digital pathology and even expanded to medical imaging at large. The collaboration has also sparked discussions on essential ethical and technical considerations for securely and reliably implementing federated learning in the domain of biomedical imaging. The outcomes of this project may serve as a blueprint for the development of other federated learning applications in the domain of biomedical imaging. The central region of the Seyfert galaxy NGC 7213 has exhibited unique and dynamic behavior in its X-ray emissions, deviating from typical active galactic nuclei (AGN) patterns. By utilizing the high-resolution grating on board the Chandra X-ray Observatory, researchers have identified both O VII and O VIII emission lines originating from both the galaxy's hot plasma and its surrounding shock waves. The analysis of the O VII line at specific wavelengths revealed two distinct components, one aligning with the galaxy's disk and a hotter one at approximately 2.5 million degrees Celsius originating from the disk itself. This hotter plasma is believed to be the result of non-radiative processes such as convection, suggesting that energy is being transferred from the black hole to its surroundings through a hot breeze. The rate at which matter is being transferred, estimated to be around 0.05 solar masses per year, is thought to be driven by this hot breeze, which in turn creates the observed shock waves and modifies the X-ray emissions in the galaxy. The observed hot breeze and shock dynamics in NGC 7213 provide valuable insights into the feedback mechanism between a supermassive black hole and its surroundings, potentially shedding light on the galaxy's evolution. The observed phenomenon may also imply that feedback from a hot breeze could be a more significant process than previously thought in regulating the growth of supermassive black holes. In systems with nonlinear dynamics, a discrete action space is often employed to improve practical applicability, however it results in a limited number of possible outcomes, which in many cases, does not satisfy the requirements of real-world systems with their continuous nature. This research proposes a joint training approach that combines data-driven policy gradient methods with globally convergent nonlinear optimization to tackle the problem of reducing costs in linear system regulators with constraints in real-time. To start, an actor-critic policy network is developed to approximate the optimal control action given the system's current state, which is then used within an iterative algorithm that performs online reinforcement learning followed by model predictive control to generate the best control action. This process is repeated until sufficient cost reduction is achieved. To accelerate learning, two-phase reinforcement learning is suggested where prior knowledge of the system is leveraged by transforming it into a batch reinforcement learning problem. Experimental findings on DC-DC buck converter and AVR system validate the proposed algorithm's ability to reduce costs in real-time while maintaining stability and adhering to constraints. This algorithm exhibits promising characteristics of model-free systems with capabilities of handling uncertainties and switching nonlinearities while providing interpretable results due to its dependence on system-specific features. Moreover, its two-batch two-phase structure enables the system to transition smoothly between the reinforcement learning and model predictive control phases with minimal disruption to overall performance. This research opens up avenues for practical model-free control applications in complex nonlinear systems with continuous outcomes through the integration of reinforcement learning and online optimization. Additionally, it is expected to contribute positively to the control of power electronic systems and similar nonlinear systems with their inherent continuous nature. Further research will be conducted to extend the scope of this work to cover a broader class of nonlinear systems with their unique characteristics. Satellite imagery plays a vital role in global environmental monitoring, yet its application is hindered by the complexity and diversity of remote sensing data. To effectively leverage this information, researchers and practitioners require accessible and integrated datasets that streamline feature extraction and model training, enabling a broader range of professionals to contribute to environmental monitoring. To address this challenge, we introduce EarthNets, an open-source framework that unifies diverse remote sensing datasets and provides streamlined feature extraction and model training capabilities. By utilizing PyTorch and offering pre-built models, data augmentations, and a comprehensive API, EarthNets empowers users to tackle a wide range of planet observation tasks across computer vision, deep learning, and other domains. With a user-friendly GitHub repository, we invite the research community to collaborate and demonstrate the capabilities of EarthNets through visualizations and experiments. Additionally, we highlight numerous real-world applications and provide code examples for key planet observation tasks. Furthermore, we organize an image classification challenge, known as PlanetNet, to crowd-source innovative solutions and foster community growth. More details can be found at our website: https://earthnets.github.io/. Identifying irregularities in streaming data is crucial for preserving the accuracy of future insights, yet current methods often struggle with accurately detecting anomalies in rapidly evolving data streams. Although they effectively pinpoint anomalies in real-time, their scalability is compromised, rendering them impractical for large-scale applications. To address this challenge, we present ReAD, a local anomaly detection framework that uses a data partitioning method across varying time scales to strike a balance between precision and efficiency. By grouping data dynamically and selecting the most relevant subsets for processing, ReAD outperforms leading techniques while achieving substantial performance enhancements, showcasing up to 90% faster processing speeds and 5% improved accuracy compared to the next best method. ReAD's versatility is further showcased through its successful applications in multiple case studies, outperforming industry-standard methods in identifying irregularities in traffic patterns, medical data, and stock market trends. With its ability to effectively detect anomalies in real-time while ensuring scalability, ReAD offers a reliable solution for accurately processing large volumes of data in real-world applications. to traditional abstract syntax trees, providing a solid foundation for neural network-based
program analysis. In this study, we introduce a cutting-edge graph neural network model

When considering only mature galaxies, this connection appears unaffected by galaxy size or shape. Conversely, when including younger galaxies, those with larger sizes or circular shapes tend to have more massive halos than expected. A major issue with Federated Learning has been the substantial time requirement for synchronizing client and server, which often leads to clients disconnecting. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel Federated Learning approach called Communication-Effective Federated Distillation. Our approach transforms the traditional Federated Learning distillation method into a multi-stage process, allowing clients to send aggregated, distilled data to the server instead of individual models. We also introduce an efficient data transmission technique based on quantization that significantly reduces data size without compromising model accuracy. Our approach is flexible and compatible with various existing models as well as different data distributions. Our experiments using multiple datasets and models showcase the time savings achievable through our approach without compromising performance. For example, model updates on the EMNIST dataset can be transmitted 20 times more frequently than before with comparable accuracy. Our approach thus efficiently mitigates the synchronization problem in Federated Learning. With continuous model updates, the server can accurately reconstruct the original model even if clients disconnect. Our approach transforms the traditional Federated Learning distillation method into a dynamic, adaptive process, allowing the server to adapt to changing models on disconnected clients and successfully deploy complex models on demanding datasets. Furthermore, we have successfully implemented our approach on real-world applications, demonstrating its ability to run efficiently on mobile devices while achieving comparable model accuracy to local training. We develop an approach to learn effective utility functions for multi-objective optimization, leveraging prior knowledge incorporated into genetic utility functions. Our method, involving utility function learning via differential evolution, enables us: 1) to introduce prior expertise through sample solutions, 2) to improve convergence towards desirable outcomes, and 3) to enhance solution quality and diversity. Utility function learning is crucial in multi-objective evolutionary algorithms but often relies on time-consuming manual specification, hindering the algorithm's potential. We illustrate the efficacy of our proposed approach, Prior Utilitarian DE, through benchmark results and a real-world case study in multi-objective design optimization, showcasing that it outperforms established evolutionary algorithms that learn utility functions or require no prior knowledge. Furthermore, Prior Utilitarian DE offers interpretability by revealing the learned utility functions and enables its components to be fine-tuned as open-source hyperparameters. Our work contributes to the evolution of utility function learning in multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, bridging the gap between those that require expert knowledge and those that autonomously learn it. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/ricardofc/priorutlied. This research is part of a broader effort to integrate prior knowledge into evolutionary algorithms, promoting their transferability and effectiveness in a wide range of applications [1]. Future research will explore prior knowledge forms other than solution sets and examine various forms of prior knowledge that can inform utility functions. Additionally, we plan to extend Prior Utilitarian DE to handle utility functions with multiple decision variables and apply it to more practical design problems, incorporating constraints when feasible. Another potential area of study is the utility function space, which could be explored using techniques like clustering or dimensionality reduction to facilitate its analysis and provide insights into the algorithm's behavior. Our work may also contribute to the development of transfer learning in evolutionary algorithms, enabling prior knowledge-based and learning-based methods to complement each other. Ultimately, we aim to make evolutionary algorithms more versatile, efficient, and effective in a variety of domains. Knowledge transfer and utilization are key research objectives that can be achieved through techniques like Prior Knowledge in Evolutionary Algorithms. These methods promote algorithm understanding, improve their performance, and foster research into how evolutionary algorithms learn and adapt to new domains. Future research will investigate how to leverage prior knowledge in algorithm design and whether incorporating it affects the algorithms' creativity and ability to discover novel solutions. Moreover, we will study the ethical implications of utilizing prior knowledge, which may result in biased outcomes, and explore ways to integrate fairness constraints into evolutionary algorithms. Recent research has focused on protecting machine learning models from adversarial attacks, with significant progress in this area. However, attacks on models trained with reinforcement learning (RL) remain an understudied area. This research proposes a novel type of attack on RL models, involving an attacker who observes the agent's interactions with the environment and provides misleading feedback to maximize the temporal shift between the agent's current and future states. Since current attacks on RL models require access to the model's source code and interaction with the environment, this research presents a new type of attack with these limitations. An RL model countermeasure is also proposed to reduce the impact of these attacks by providing temporal constraints in feedback updates to the agent. This countermeasure is effective in limiting the attack's impact while still allowing the agent to learn effectively. Additionally, our study highlights the importance of attacks with limited knowledge, outperforming previously developed attacks with access to the model's source code and environment. This research contributes to the advancement of adversarial attacks on RL models and provides a framework for future research. Our research focuses on the properties of a specific two-dimensional lattice designed using a non-symmorphic wallpaper group, in which Dirac points can be positioned and the speed of electrons passing through them can be controlled. By modifying the lattice structure using four different methods, we demonstrate that this control can be extended to all Dirac points within the lattice. Furthermore, our findings reveal that only certain adjustments enable the movement of Dirac points across the lattice, while making others results in these points accumulating at high-energy zones. Additionally, our study explores the topological characteristics of the lattice and identifies various phases, which can be distinguished by symmetry from non-symmorphic and non-trivial topological properties. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for managing Dirac points in electronic systems built using adjustable high-symmetry points, which could potentially lead to innovative technologies.

In non-stationary reinforcement learning with risk aversion, the environment's policy-dependent reward and transition probabilities change over time while an agent seeks to maximize a variant of long-term expected utility known as the total expected future value (TEFV). The parameter $\gamma$ in the TEFV function controls an agent's level of risk aversion, with higher values indicating greater caution. The key performance metric in this context is dynamic regret, which measures an agent's relative shortfall in rewards compared to an optimal decision-making strategy. Building on recent breakthroughs in non-stationary reinforcement learning, the authors develop an algorithm that achieves the first known rate of $O(\log(T)/\log(\gamma))$ dynamic regret in risk-aware reinforcement learning environments with changing transition and reward profiles. This result holds for environments in which the set of possible actions remains constant and an agent can adapt an infinite sequence of policies through online learning. The algorithm's performance is validated through a novel analysis of an online learning problem, which also yields an efficient method for identifying an environment's structure in non-stationary reinforcement learning settings. The authors' research further refutes a previous assumption that risk-averse reinforcement learning with dynamic environments and changing reward profiles cannot be optimized efficiently. Our analysis focuses on the interdependence between problem reports and includes analysis of a problem's characteristics, its relationship with other issues, and how it changes over time. This dataset offers researchers a valuable resource for developing and testing new methodologies in software analytics. Due to the complexity and variability of problem tracking data, we provide a detailed description of our data collection process and highlight potential research avenues based on our dataset's features. In distributed machine learning, aggregating information from multiple machines is typically achieved through methods like arithmetic mean aggregation, yet research has demonstrated that this approach may not always lead to an accurate solution, particularly when machines work with noisy data on complex tasks. To overcome this limitation, a new collection of aggregation methods known as Semi-Continuous Non-Linear (SCN) aggregation functions has been developed, which guarantees the convergence to an accurate solution regardless of the data quality or system complexities. The paper introduces SCN functions, highlights their unique properties and demonstrate their effectiveness in solving distributed machine learning problems. Furthermore, SCN functions can also address challenges in other fields such as aggregation in multiple agent systems, thus broadening the scope of applications. The research presents theoretical justifications for using SCN functions and conducts comprehensive experiments to validate their performance. The findings show that SCN functions lead to more precise results compared to traditional mean aggregation method in deep learning applications, such as image classification and object detection, using popular datasets such as ImageNet and MS-COCO, especially in complex scenarios with limited communication bandwidth and large datasets. The source code is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/alexandar-alex/distributed-deep-learning/tree/main/scn_aggregation. This research presents an advanced method for creating polymers based on a cutting-edge technique that leverages artificial neural networks in chemistry. The technique uses data from molecular structure analysis and a high-performance computational tool to calculate key chemical properties. By applying a sophisticated algorithm to multiple predictions, our method identifies the ideal molecular structure for a target substance, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in creating polymers with desired properties. Notably, the technique can handle complex molecules with high accuracy even when relying on pre-trained models, and we showcase its capabilities in designing novel polymers with exceptional mechanical properties. Specifically, our research enables the creation of materials with impact resistance 50% stronger than Kevlar and flexural strength 30% greater than carbon fiber. By combining machine learning and optimization techniques, we successfully derived polymers with superior properties, and our tool is versatile and can be tailored to produce molecules with a range of desired properties in the non-linear region of the prediction space. This research presents a method called direct transcription for dynamic enhancement (DTDE) to amplify the effects of therapeutic treatments, such as respiratory therapy, through control of the diaphragm. The study employs a mathematical model that simulates the movement of two patients' lungs, modeled as spherical containers, with and without the intervention of respiratory therapy. The model's outputs are compared to experimental data from patients with and without respiratory issues, obtained through X-ray imaging. The goal is to identify the inputs that produce the most beneficial outcomes, according to a cost function that measures the volume of the lungs and the stability of the patients' heads. The research uses a technique called model predictive control (MPC) to test various inputs and finds the most effective settings, resulting in improved lung volumes and reduced sway in the patients' heads. The application of DTDE and MPC has the potential to improve treatment planning for respiratory therapy and expand the use of MPC beyond autonomous systems to also enhance human well-being. The research provides a step-by-step guide on using MPC and DTDE, with accompanying software and mathematical models available online for other researchers to use. The findings highlight the challenges and potential pitfalls of using MPC and DTDE to make decisions with incomplete information, with limitations due to the simplicity of the model and the limitations of the data. The research opens up avenues for future research to develop more realistic models and improve decision-making with a deeper understanding of the dynamics of the patients' lungs. In modern manufacturing, energy efficiency is a critical factor, and achieving real-world improvements requires precise methods. To this end, a cutting-edge approach using Bayesian evaluation and evolutionary techniques has been developed to enhance power usage assessment in machining centers, yielding significant reductions - up to 3.5 kW in this particular case. This innovative method builds on a conventional power modeling framework, offering a reliable statistical foundation and fast deployment capabilities, while also facilitating the identification of optimal parameter-correlated power consumption profiles. Furthermore, the method enables the creation of enhanced power models tailored to specific workpieces, as demonstrated through simulations and practical tests using a CNC milling machine. To validate the method's effectiveness, a comprehensive set of experiments was conducted, involving 160 runs with different parameters, and compared against a traditional method using neural networks, which it substantially outperformed. This advancement has the potential to translate into substantial cost savings in the machining industry. Additionally, the method can be adapted for use in power-intensive systems, and its source code will be made available upon request. This research aims to inspire further optimization initiatives in the machining sector. Several avenues for further investigation have been identified, including the application of this method to detect energy-wasting patterns and develop more sophisticated machining strategies centered on power efficiency. Moreover, the results of this study may be extended to related domains, such as electrical drives and domestic appliances, where similar challenges apply. Finally, the implementation of this method could contribute to a positive environmental impact by reducing energy consumption in these industries. To summarize, this research presents an innovative solution to the complex problem of power usage assessment in machining centers, offering a reliable statistical foundation, fast deployment capabilities, and improved performance. The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is typically defined as the exponent that describes how quickly the expected displacement of a randomly walking particle grows over time. This paper explores the relationship between this dimension and a measure developed by Mattila and Sahari on infinite graphs, which has connections to conformal iterates of a given Ahlfors regular measure. We demonstrate that if a graph satisfies certain regularity conditions and has finite outer measure, its spectral dimension can be determined based on the conformal dimension of the graph's geometric representation, which in turn depends on its Ahlfors regular measure. Additionally, we provide a simplified proof of the theorem by Serra and Strain that related these dimensions to the Lagrange multiplier in graph Laplacian eigenvalue problems. Finally, we examine the applicability of these theorems to specific examples, such as planar maps and certain self-similar graphs, and show that they provide new insights into these spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain planar maps have a spectral dimension greater than one, even though they have a conformal dimension less than two, and that certain self-similar graphs have a spectral dimension equal to one, even though they have a conformal dimension greater than one. These results provide evidence that the spectral dimension may not always be comparable to the conformal dimension on infinite graphs. Furthermore, they raise questions about the relationship between these dimensions and the parabolicity of the graph, as well as its geometric regularity. To answer these questions, we developed a new criterion that relates the conformal dimension to the regularity of a graph's geometric representation, which may be of independent interest. Specifically, we showed that if a graph satisfies certain regularity conditions, then its conformal dimension is greater than or equal to one if and only if its geometric regularity is greater than or equal to one. Using this new criterion, we were able to explain why certain planar maps have a spectral dimension greater than one, even though they have a conformal dimension less than two. Additionally, we examined the applicability of these theorems to specific examples, such as planar maps with vanishing outer measure, and showed that they provide new insights into these spaces. Specifically, we demonstrated that these maps have a spectral dimension greater than one, even though they have a conformal dimension less than two, and that this result provides evidence that the spectral dimension may not always be comparable to the conformal dimension on infinite graphs that have a finite outer measure. This research investigates the distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability of electronic signatures created using the TouchSign system, which we found to be more secure than other existing methods that rely on static image-based signatures. Our study showcases the value of acoustic signal-based signatures in providing an additional layer of security compared to traditional static signatures. The findings of our research are crucial for informing the development of reliable authentication technologies. This research introduces an innovative content-based Graph Privacy Consultant (GPC) to enhance the privacy of visually identifiable individuals within graph-based images. GPC leverages a custom-trained model, which segregates images into visually sensitive areas containing specific individuals, thereby enabling the application of tailored privacy measures. Its effectiveness is showcased through its incorporation in two cutting-edge generative adversarial network (GAN) methods, revealing its ability to amplify existing privacy improvements. Furthermore, our experimental findings highlight the efficacy of GPC in maintaining overall image quality while reducing the discriminative power on various benchmark datasets. Lastly, to facilitate seamless integration with existing graph-based image analysis models, GPC is framed as a post-processing module. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhaozhengui/GPC/.

We examine the concept of hidden purity in probability and possibility theory, incorporating it into our understanding of probability measures and vague predicates within possible world semantics for modal and epistemic logic. Hidden purity in probability theory is analogous to having only minimal support when considered through the lens of interval-valued probability theory. In possible world semantics for modal and epistemic logic, hidden purity transpires due to epistemic or modal accessibility relations that encompass time or are not fully retrospective. This idea is applicable to both classical and intuitionistic logics, with implications extending to quantum mechanics, specifically the measurement process, and the distinction between approximate and exact knowledge. Furthermore, we investigate properties of hidden purity in relation to other logical concepts such as possibility and necessity. Additionally, we present models of concealed purity, incorporating them into nonstandard probability theory and possible world semantics. Finally, we discuss potential directions for further research.

The CP2K program package, often used in atomistic simulations, exhibits exceptional performance on various platforms due to its efficiency and high scalability. This is evident from its achievements at the 48th International Symposium on Fault-Tolerant Distributed Algorithms (FTDCS 2019), where it successfully processed simulations totaling approximately 1.12 exaflops on machines like JUQUEEN and SierraA100. This report aims to provide a detailed overview of CP2K's capabilities and recent advancements that have enabled its success, including enhancements in the treatment of electrons and their interaction with nuclei. Furthermore, we present scaling results from the Tier-0 platforms, including JUQUEEN, SierraA100, and Frontera, showcasing CP2K's potential to harness the power of exascale computing. This report serves as a comprehensive guide for users who wish to achieve scalable simulations, and it also serves as a technical document that can be accessed through the CP2K website. Finally, we highlight the avenues for future research influenced by our findings, particularly in the domains of post-Moore law electronics and advanced materials development.

We introduce a novel task called Cross-Camera Deep Tinting, where we develop an end-to-end approach to change hair colors in videos across different cameras by only using a single reference model. Our method novelly employs pixel-matching statistics to create a shared representation of images and videos captured by distinct cameras, thus enabling cross-camera color manipulation. To further enhance its practicality, we based our approach on efficient neural networks, allowing it to process high-resolution inputs efficiently. Our experimental findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in producing accurate and visually appealing results that can be achieved quickly. We also conducted a user study and found that participants' preferences on our method are evenly divided between those who prefer high-quality results and those who prioritize speed. The widespread adoption of software development across diverse sectors has created numerous opportunities for researchers to study coding practices.  GitHub's vast repository of open-source code provides a rich environment for researchers to conduct empirical studies on software maintenance, but analyzing this data is often plagued by difficulties stemming from file naming ambiguities, version inconsistencies, and fragmented metadata.  This research presents an innovative approach to address these challenges by utilizing advanced machine learning techniques to identify files with equivalent content across different repositories, and then applying these results to derive meaningful metadata from GitHub repositories by aggregating information from files with similar names.  This methodology enables researchers to derive a reliable summary of repository metadata, and showcases its potential to contribute to existing knowledge on software maintenance.  Additionally, the framework's underlying model and findings are accessible through an online platform.  This study's outcomes offer fresh insights into software development practices, while also highlighting potential limitations and areas for further investigation.  Ultimately, this research aims to inspire future studies to investigate various aspects of software maintenance through a more unified and comprehensive analysis of GitHub's repository data. This study examines the fractional Yamabe flow's behavior over a wide range of data and finds that it either converges slowly or remains stationary. Additionally, we demonstrate the flow's existence and analyze its long-term properties, establishing conditions under which it converges to either a Type-I or Type-II metric in the large. Our findings show that the flow converges to a Ricci-flat metric in thin neighborhoods of compact data, and it remains stationary for data that is both compact and close to being Ricci-flat. Furthermore, we establish that the flow converges to a conical metric in a broad category of data that includes those with isolated singularities. Specifically, if the singularity's order is less than 1/2 and its mass is finite, the flow converges to a conical metric with a small neck and a large central region that approximates accurately. Our work also explores the universality of the flow's orbits and potential moduli spaces, and it reveals that the flow either converges slowly or remains stationary in a wide range of data. Our findings have implications for the study of the moduli space of positive scalar curvature metrics, and they suggest the presence of an intricate geometric structure that underlies this space, with many of its features reflecting the properties of conical metrics. new cooperative recommendation approach that can handle multi-sparse-domain scenarios.

When dealing with noisy samples, providing guarantees for convergence in high-dimensional least squares regression is a complex challenge. This paper addresses this issue by introducing two aspects of reliability for least squares estimation.

Firstly, it is proven that under specific conditions, having access to sufficient in advance information about noise levels allows for the determination of a threshold below which the least squares estimator achieves optimal rates of convergence in a minimum-expectation framework.

Secondly, this paper explores retrospective guarantees, offering explicit assurances that the least squares estimator will converge to the true model with a predetermined level of confidence, even in high-dimensional scenarios, provided that a sufficient number of samples are collected.

In situations where an agent observes other beings performing a task, it can gain insight into the underlying objectives that drove those actions, a process known as intrinsic motivation theory. However, real-life scenarios often present complications by incorporating elements like partial oversight, where an observer isn't fully privy to the target being's goals, leading to ambiguous signals in the observed behavior. To address this challenge, we've developed a step-by-step approach to decipher the target being's objectives, even in the face of partial oversight, using an observer's internal simulation model, which serves as a reliable indicator of the target being's goals. To facilitate this simulation, we've created a framework that models the target being's objectives as a spectrum of possible goals and an observer's confidence within this spectrum as a measure of uncertainty, both of which are key components in a Bayesian learning model, allowing the observer to continually refine its understanding of the target being's objectives over time. We've put our framework to the test in a 2D grid-world environment, where an observer attempts to determine a target being's goal that involves retrieving a valuable item while navigating through a maze, all under the observer's partial oversight. We've compared our framework's performance with two alternative methods: one that assumes complete oversight and another that uses a simplified model to simulate a target being's objectives. To our delight, our framework emerged as the most effective in accurately identifying a target being's goals even in the face of partial oversight. We've also observed that an observer's confidence in its understanding of a target being's objectives can serve as a reliable metric to gauge the observer's own level of uncertainty, thus providing a direct benefit to the observer. We consider a nontrivial, orientable surface of genus at least one and equip it with a metric that varies arbitrarily. Any subgroup of the surface's fundamental group can be represented by a metrically finite collection of loops whose union forms the entire genus g surface. Select one loop from each subgroup; then we examine the robustness of the resulting set of loops when the surface's metric changes. Under certain conditions, this set exhibits robust connectivity and scales proportionally with the number of subgroups; in specific scenarios, it even encompasses the entire boundary of the Veech surface's associated tunnel system, demonstrating that this set is not capped by any finite collection of loops. Notably, our findings counter previous assumptions presented in arXiv:1812.05491. Additionally, our work's implications extend to geodesic lattices within hyperbolic surfaces, and we provide supporting visual examples for our conclusions. Lastly, we pose an open question regarding robust small loop transfer regions within hyperbolic surfaces more broadly. A critical problem in Industry 4.0 is efficiently managing production lines to meet changing demand for varied products. To address this, we developed a control method that can simultaneously produce multiple items with differing parameters, such as specifications and quantities. To ensure manufacturing quality, our approach incorporates strict constraints into the control process. However, control problems involving difficult controls pose a significant challenge, leading to suboptimal solutions that may not meet product quality standards or yield full economic benefits. To resolve this issue, we propose a two-step deep reinforcement learning method, which decouples the control problem into separate estimation and control processes. The first step uses reinforcement learning to estimate parameters based on feedback from the environment, while the second step leverages these parameters to calculate optimal controls. Our method was successfully validated using an example related to laser welding processes commonly used in the automotive industry, where we demonstrated improved control solutions and increased production flexibility. Notably, our approach achieved results comparable to those of advanced industrial planning methods but required significantly less computational effort. Furthermore, our method enables the integration of various manufacturing strategies, enabling production systems to adapt to changing market conditions and prioritize specific products or processes. With ongoing advancements in machine learning and sensor technologies, our approach can be applied to a wide range of complex manufacturing systems. To facilitate this, we provide our code and simulation data on public platforms for the purpose of collaborative research. Specifically, our code is available on GitHub and our data can be accessed via the OpenResearch portal. To ensure the transparency and reproducibility of our research, we detailed our data preparation procedures, simulation experiments, and results in an accompanying report available on the arXiv platform. Additionally, our results are also summarized in an article published in the Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing. To ensure the quality and reliability of our research, our work was thoroughly reviewed and validated by multiple experts in the relevant field. Specifically, our research was reviewed by experts from the University of Stuttgart, the Technical University of Berlin, and the Technical University of Munich, among others. To promote the dissemination of our research, we presented our findings at multiple conferences, including the 2020 IEEE Conference on Industrial Automation and the 2020 IEEE Conference on Industrial Technology. To facilitate the practical implementation of our research, we established a partnership with the automotive company, BMW Group, who provided valuable feedback and guidance throughout our study. To ensure the continuity and sustainability of our research, we established a research project focused on the control of laser-based manufacturing processes, where we will investigate novel applications and research questions related to this topic.

This paper is the second in a series that investigates how black hole mass evolved over cosmic time. In the first paper, we established that low-mass black holes follow a distinct mass distribution pattern. In this follow-up, we examine higher-mass black holes, including those resulting from direct collapse. We employed a comprehensive computational model to derive a unified description of black hole mass distributions across all sizes, from the most massive to the smallest. This theoretical framework is in agreement with real-world observations of supermassive black holes in the current universe and also predicts accurately the rates at which supermassive black holes should have formed and existed throughout the universe's history. Furthermore, our unified model can also be applied to analyze the properties of black holes formed through distinct physical processes, such as star formation and direct collapse, and it indicates that the latter contributes significantly to the universe's population of more massive black holes below a certain threshold. We discovered that the probability of direct collapse yielding a supermassive black hole at a given time should be the same as the probability of a star forming a black hole through the standard stellar process. As a result, while direct collapse has played a crucial role in seeding the universe's first supermassive black holes, its influence diminishes over time and it no longer affects the formation of supermassive black holes in the current universe. Instead, it is the black holes formed from stars that contribute to the population of supermassive black holes in the present universe. We found that the probability of a star forming a black hole through the standard stellar process that should exist at a given time should be the same as the probability of direct collapse yielding a supermassive black hole. This relationship holds for black holes of all masses, from those that should have existed at the universe's birth to those that should exist at its end. The underlying physics of condensed matter systems can be thoroughly investigated using inelastic neutron scattering, where the intensity of scattered neutrons is influenced by specific excitations within the system. However, data collected from this process is complex and requires interpretation in the context of the system's dynamics. To facilitate this understanding, we employ deep neural networks to establish a direct correlation between the three-dimensional data collected from inelastic neutron scattering and the corresponding excitations within the system. To ensure our model remains transparent and reliable, we utilize transparent variants of convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Notably, our findings demonstrate that these models can accurately replicate the excitation spectrum of a system with simpler structures and those exhibiting symmetry, thereby showcasing their effectiveness in inelastic neutron scattering data analysis. Furthermore, we show that these models can be modified to focus on specific aspects of a system's dynamics, where their transparent nature significantly enhances their interpretability when compared to conventional neural networks. With continued advancements in experimental techniques and data collection, neural networks will play an increasingly pivotal role in the systematic analysis of complex data across various fields. Consequently, we emphasize the importance of employing transparent neural networks that can effectively convey their decision-making process, especially when dealing with sensitive or critical applications. To support our research, we have made our code and data available for public access at https://github.com/NeuralINS/INS\_data\_analysis. Additionally, 3D visualizations of our data and results can be found at https://neuronixx.github.io/NeuralINS/index.html. Lastly, the raw data used in this study is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.20361/insdc0000001 and https://doi.org/10.20361/insdc0000002. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), characterized by multiple principal elements and random atomic arrangements, are renowned for their exceptional mechanical properties and versatility. With their potential to outperform conventional alloys, HEAs are gaining significant attention. Traditional methods for developing and evaluating HEAs often rely on extensive, time-consuming experimental trials. This research aims to synapse these efforts by leveraging machine learning and other data analytics techniques to analyze existing datasets and forecast future developments in HEA properties. While machine learning has shown considerable promise in materials science, it still grapples with the inherent complexity and variability of materials. This review seeks to illuminate the progress, obstacles, and potential avenues for integrating machine learning in HEA research. It also seeks to inspire novel applications and foster collaboration across the machine-learning-materials community. With growing confidence, machine learning can become a pivotal tool for designing and optimizing materials, thereby revolutionizing the development of high-performing materials. This review is intended for researchers seeking to comprehend the underlying principles and applications of machine learning in materials science. By consolidating existing knowledge, it may serve as a valuable entry point for researchers looking to apply machine learning to solve problems in HEAs and contribute to the advancement of this field. Additionally, it may provide valuable insights for researchers working on other materials systems. Furthermore, this review seeks to stimulate innovative ideas for integrating machine learning in materials science, with a specific focus on high-entropy alloys. To that end, it poses several open questions and challenges, with potential solutions that could propel the field forward. These include developing more sophisticated neural networks that can accurately predict mechanical properties and their underlying mechanisms, as well as designing more efficient and robust correlation-estimation models. Moreover, there is a pressing need to establish standardized protocols for collecting, integrating, and updating large datasets from diverse experimental and computational sources. By addressing these challenges, researchers can unlock the full potential of machine learning to accelerate the design, development, and deployment of next-generation high-entropy alloys and other advanced materials. This review may also be of interest to researchers working in related fields of materials science, where machine learning is transforming our understanding of materials and our ability to design them. With its potential to outperform conventional materials, high-entropy alloys are poised to revolutionize various industries, including aerospace, automotive, and energy production. By integrating machine learning, we can harness the power of big data and computational models to accelerate the design and development of high-entropy alloys and other advanced materials. This research may inspire novel applications and foster collaboration across the machine-learning-materials

The non-Gaussian continuous nature of binary matrix elements poses a significant challenge, making the determinant's calculation impractical in many cases, hence researchers resort to the matrix's rank as a suitable alternative, known as the matrix's margin, which is defined as the minimum across-row and column-based support counts. Due to the hard nature of converting binary elements to Gaussian values, a non-uniform sampling method for binary matrices based on their rank has yet to be developed. Our proposed algorithm utilizes a modified version of the sequential importance sampling technique to efficiently generate binary random matrices of a specified rank and size with distribution $p(\mathbf{M}) \propto \exp(-\alpha \mathsf{Sc}(\mathbf{M}))$, where $\mathsf{Sc}(\mathbf{M})$ is the sum of the matrix's row and column supports, and $\alpha$ is a positive constant. Our approach incorporates two techniques to achieve high efficiency: the efficient computation of the marginal distribution using the dynamic programming method and the early determination of the sampling history's validity. Our method has been successfully applied to the design of linear codes with specified error-correcting capabilities through binary matrices. Our experimental results demonstrate that our sampling algorithm outperforms existing methods by generating matrices at a rate 3-4 times faster than the rejection method. At the same time, our code is written in C++ and is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/alexandermartinez/BinaryMarginSampling. Additionally, a pre-compiled version of the code is available at https://github.com/alexandermartinez/BinaryMarginCodeSampler. It is also worth noting that our work has been inspired by a problem in the coding community, and we believe that our sampling algorithm will have applications beyond coding due to its broad applicability. Furthermore, we have successfully applied our sampling algorithm to design codes with specified error-correcting capabilities, and we have even found the best known codes that can correct up to $17$ errors out of $32$ using our sampling algorithm's implementation. Our work's impact is further illustrated by the fact that our sampling algorithm has enabled us to find the best known codes with error-correcting capabilities, and we have even developed an open-source software framework that allows users to design linear codes with specified error-correcting capabilities using our sampling algorithm. We've developed a new method to create equally spaced optical frequency combs using microresonators, which enables precise adjustment of the comb's tooth spacing. By applying a uniform thermal shift to the microresonator, the eigenfrequencies of its fundamental modes change proportionally, resulting in evenly spaced comb teeth. The parametric modulation of the microresonator's transmission spectrum reveals the potential modes of the comb and allows for the synchronization of their frequencies. The proposed technique facilitates the exploration of four-wave mixing in microresonators and offers potential applications in generating optical frequency division multiplexing systems and coherent supercontinua. Additionally, it enables the exploration of other physical systems with similar nonlinear properties, such as Josephson junction arrays or waveguide lattice systems. The adjustable comb spacing ranges from tens to thousands of megahertz, with a maximum accuracy of less than 0.01 kHz in the lab. We establish that in any acylindrically hyperbolic group G, there exists a randomly generated subgroup using a probabilistic method drawn from a probability measure that prioritizes smaller subgroups and is invariant under G. This allows us to prove that such a subgroup is stable, loyal, and non-trivial, thereby addressing an open question concerning the existence of loyal invariant random subgroups in acylindrically hyperbolic groups. Additionally, our approach provides a streamlined proof for the existence of non-trivial, relatively soluble, and G-invariant subgroups within any acylindrically hyperbolic group. Our work further includes an analysis demonstrating that the likelihood of a generated subgroup being relatively soluble can be adjusted by introducing an optional parameter that influences the membership probability. Lastly, our findings suggest that the ratio of the subgroup's rank to its size should asymptotically approach 1 as the group's size increases. Conversely, if the subgroup's rank is significantly smaller than its size, we introduce a parameter that controls the likelihood of non-soluble generators; this parameter can be made arbitrarily large under conditions where the subgroup's rank is substantially smaller than its size. Our research provides a probabilistic solution to creating non-trivial, relatively soluble, and G-invariant subgroups in acylindrically hyperbolic groups and sheds light on the relationship between the subgroup's rank and size. Our analysis also raises questions about the feasibility of generating subgroups with specific characteristics and offers potential avenues for exploration. Our work also establishes that the probabilistic method used can be adapted to create non-trivial, relatively soluble, and G-invariant subgroups in any acylindrically hyperbolic group; this approach can likely be extended to other classes of groups that possess similar properties. Our work also establishes that our probabilistic method can be adjusted to prioritize non-soluble generators by altering the likelihood of membership. Quantization has been proven to significantly reduce the computational resources required by deep neural networks with no noticeable decline in their performance. Nonetheless, the underlying rationale behind its beneficial effects on generalization capabilities remains unclear. This research aims to provide insights into this phenomenon by focusing on binary weight neural networks and exploring their Nonlinear Kernel Transform (NTK). We demonstrate that binary weight networks have an intrinsic property that restricts the norm of their weight matrix, which in turn influences the eigenvalues of their NTK. Consequently, this property contributes to improved generalization. Moreover, our findings also reveal that the beneficial effect of quantization on generalization can be achieved through the reduction of model width (number of neurons) at a given layer, which provides a practical approach for practitioners seeking improved generalization performance while adhering to strict computational constraints. Our research was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, utilizing binary weight neural networks in conjunction with the straight-through-estimation technique for activation quantization. The results show that the width of binary weight networks can be effectively utilized for the control of generalization performance, which is in line with our theoretical findings. Additionally, we observed that the optimal width of these networks exhibits a significant decline in complex models, which further underscores the practical value of our research. It is worth noting that our research focused on binary weight neural networks but similar principles can be applied to other forms of quantized weight neural networks. Our theoretical model, along with the accompanying code, is available for public access at https://github.com/zhengyu-1999/Quantization.git. It can be utilized by researchers for reproducing our experimental results or developing novel ideas inspired by our research. Furthermore, we propose an open research question that could lead to groundbreaking advancements in the field, which is the automatic determination of generalization performance-driven binary weight network widths. It is anticipated that resolving this challenge will enable the widespread adoption of binary weight neural networks for the efficient computation of generalization performance. Additionally, we provide a detailed description of our research goals and the potential approaches for addressing this challenge in Section 5 of our research paper. A new indicator, referred to as the intersection multiplier, is developed at specific points where branches of the stress surface intersect, allowing for the determination of the stress state at those points in solvable lattice frameworks composed of convex polyhedra with rigid material properties. This intersection multiplier is capable of identifying whether branches of the stress surface actually represent physical states of stress or are instead trivial extensions, thus enabling the reconstruction of the actual stress state at intersection points. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the intersection multiplier remains defined and provides valuable information even when the stress state at those points is indeterminate. Various numerical examples are used to illustrate its application and effectiveness. Ultimately, the intersection multiplier is shown to possess sufficient robustness to be implemented in practical engineering design using numerical methods. At intersection points where branches of the stress surface do not actually intersect but rather converge, an alternative indicator, referred to as the stress flow multiplier, is introduced to determine the stress state. This stress flow multiplier is capable of identifying the direction in which branches of the stress surface converge and is utilized to decompose the stress state at points where branches converge into unique and independent components that converge along specific paths. Furthermore, the stress flow multiplier is found to be defined at points with indeterminate stress states and is robust against numerical errors, making it applicable in practical engineering design using numerical methods. Numerical examples are used to illustrate its application and importance. The stress flow multiplier is shown to possess properties similar to those of multipliers used in other optimization methods, such as the Lagrange multiplier and the potential flow multiplier, thereby establishing a theoretical framework that bridges various concepts in stress surface analysis through their shared mathematical properties. This research investigates the Cauchy problem for the 3D Navier-Stokes equations in a periodic domain, and its equivalent modified equation within the maximum norm framework. We demonstrate the existence of a local and periodic solution that remains bounded over time, and compare its rate of change with that of a finite-element method solution achieved using the ARK-IMES scheme, which was previously shown to be unconditionally stable in the maximum norm in a previous study. The difference between these two solutions is shown to decrease over time at a rate proportional to $\exp(-\alpha t)$, with $\alpha$ representing a positive constant that can be found. Additionally, we derive an a posteriori error estimate for the 3D Bar\'i\'nton-Dirichlet problem in a periodic domain using the ARK-IMES scheme, which remains valid even in the presence of non-constant coefficients. The error estimate is shown to converge at a rate of $O(k^2)$ in time and $O(h^2)$ in space, with $k$ and $h$ representing the time and space step sizes, respectively. Furthermore, we present a method for determining a positive constant that bounds the magnitude of residual vectors on the right-hand side of the linear system resulting from discretizing the Navier-Stokes equations using the ARK-IMES scheme, which can then be used to develop an a posteriori error estimate for the direct method. The error estimate is shown to converge at a rate of $O(k^2)$ in time and $O(h^2)$ in space. Several numerical experiments are conducted to verify the accuracy of these error estimates in various scenarios. The research demonstrates that the ARK-IMES scheme offers a reliable and efficient approach to solving Navier-Stokes equations, particularly in complex periodic systems. We've developed a novel approach, using a classical verification process, which guarantees the desired outcome with high confidence. Our method boasts a linear time complexity, a significant improvement over previous techniques requiring cubic time. This advancement was facilitated by a new framework that enables efficient validation of complex probability distributions on classical systems. The development of this framework, which is based on a simple yet powerful principle, allows us to extend existing theoretical findings to practical applications within quantum algorithm verification. Additionally, our influence-aware probability theorem serves as a fundamental tool for this purpose, distinguishing to its credit the ability to provide precise guarantees in complex scenarios. Furthermore, our work introduces a new direction in probability research, where the probability of a computation is influenced by the quality of the producing circuit. Furthermore, our classical verification process may also be used to evaluate the total error probability of quantum algorithms, an area previously dominated by theoretical estimates. In complex brain systems, chimeras - hybrids of different neural states - emerge, 
whereone type of oscillation coexists with another, often contradicting the 
notion that homogeneous and heterogeneous networks harbor the same dynamics. 
Although this phenomenon has been observed in various systems, its presence 
in the brain remains uncertain, mainly because current detection methods are 
sensitive to noise and require precise initial conditions. 
This study presents a new approach to identify chimeras in spiking neural networks 
without requiring precise starting points and resistant to noise. 
This method works by distinguishing neural states based on frequency content, 
and then assesses consistency across time and variability in different runs. 
Using this strategy, global strategies can be developed to analyze various neural 
network models and parameters, thereby shedding light on the potential role 
of chimeras in the brain. Additionally, this study demonstrates how chimeras 
transition into other states, potentially serving as a basis for different 
cognitive functions. Lastly, the study explores how chimeras emerge when control 
parameters are altered, and discusses the implications of these findings for 
understanding neural dynamics. This detection method and associated analysis 
could be valuable in uncovering the role of chimeras in the brain and potentially 
exploit their function in novel therapeutic treatments. Furthermore, the 
implementation of this global detection method using open-source software could 
facilitate collaborative research into neural dynamics. Finally, the study 
highlights the potential for neural chimeras to contribute to our 
understanding- and treatment- of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Open-source software available at https://github.com/NeuralChimera/NeuralChimera.git. To assess variability in outcomes and potential biases generated by randomization techniques, specifically for planetary system evolution simulations using the REBOUND N-body code, this study employed multiple instances of Monte Carlo sampling with diverse seeds. The researchers set initial conditions for various planetary architectures, including one with a circular orbit and three with eccentricities, ranging from mild to extreme, and then ran these models with and without EXRF to compare their evolution. By comparing low-eccentricity scenarios, including a reference with no EXRF, to their high-eccentricity counterparts, the impact of EXRF became evident, with the randomization pressure resulting in decreased orbital eccentricities, $E_{\rm esc}$, and mean distances from planets to their host stars, $\langle d\rangle$. Conversely, low-eccentricity scenarios exhibited increased orbital eccentricities and mean distances following EXRF application. Notably, the researchers discovered that planets with higher initial orbital distances were more likely to experience ejection in both low-eccentricity and high-eccentricity scenarios following EXRF. Furthermore, the researchers found that the application of EXRF led to a preference for shorter orbital periods among surviving planets in all test cases. Lastly, while the researchers found that high-eccentricity scenarios exhibited increased variability in outcomes compared to their low-eccentricity counterparts, the overall pattern of behavior following EXRF remained consistent across these groups. In summary, this study demonstrates that the widespread adoption of EXRF may introduce biases in planetary evolution simulations, potentially affecting the outcome of numerous N-body codes. Moreover, the researchers found that the application of EXRF may result in the generation of artificially rare or unlikely planetary configurations over extended periods of time. Consequently, the researchers recommend incorporating an inner boundary within which planets are not perturbed by EXRF to mitigate these biases and facilitate more accurate simulations of planetary system evolution. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of thorough variability assessments when developing and implementing randomization techniques in N-body codes. Additionally, the researchers provide a code modification for REBOUND that enables the efficient performance of EXRF simulations on large datasets, including those with hundreds of planets. This code modification can be accessed via MNRAS at the corresponding author's website. Lastly, the researchers have made available a publicly viewable Google Drive folder containing the raw data generated by this study for the benefit of the scientific community. This data includes all figures, tables, and numerical data generated by the researchers, and can be accessed via the following link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1

Our research aimed to investigate how brain connectivity derived from resting-state functional MRI data at different sites can be combined to predict behavioral and clinical outcomes more accurately. To achieve this, we analyzed data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and the Chinese COBRE Human Connectome Research (CCHCR), as well as simulated data, using Bayesian cross-validation. The results showed that combining functional connectome information from multiple sites significantly enhanced our ability to predict behavioral and clinical outcomes, while site-specific effects were present but minimal. Furthermore, the HCP data yielded more precise predictions compared to the CCHCR data due to its larger sample size. Notably, the simulated data indicated that our Bayesian cross-validation method can accurately identify relationships between brain connectivity and target variables at prediction sites, despite originating from different sites. Overall, our findings highlight the practical value of multi-site collaborations in advancing our understanding of the complex relationships between brain connectivity and behavioral or clinical outcomes. Additionally, the approach employed in this study may serve as a useful tool for analyzing and integrating data from diverse collaborative research projects. The implemented code is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/Neuropsych-UIUC/BayesMultiSite. Raw data can be obtained through open-access links to the HCP and CCHCR databases, while preprocessed data can be retrieved via the HCP Data Browser. This research also presents new specifications for gradient estimates and heat diffusion processes in directed graphs with Ricci curvature constraints. Finally, we have provided a non-convex example directed network, which meets the Ricci curvature criterion but lacks concentration of measure and efficient heat transfer properties. Unlike its convex counterpart, this example exhibits distinct behavior in gradient estimates and heat transfer processes. Through this study, we hope to bridge the gap between directed graph representations and lower Ricci curvature bounds in differential geometry and Dirichlet problems, heat equations, and concentration of measure phenomena. A significant portion of social media communication involves code-mixed languages, where multiple languages are combined within the same utterance. This linguistic phenomenon is prevalent across numerous countries and is particularly prominent in India, where Hindi is code-mixed with English. To effectively process code-mixed languages, researchers have proposed various techniques, although many still rely on data from non-code-mixed languages to supplement the training. To address this limitation, our work introduces a new approach that dynamically identifies transition points between languages within a code-mixed sentence and generates position-specific encodings accordingly. Experiment results reveal that our model surpasses benchmarks in multiple evaluation metrics. To facilitate replicating our research, we have open-sourced our implementation. Additionally, to promote further study, we have made our data preprocessing tools accessible as well. Both resources can be accessed at https://github.com/amanbasu/HINMIX-PESTO. Our model's performance is particularly noteworthy in sentiment analysis and part-of-speech tagging, achieving gains of 0.14 and 0.12 F1-score respectively, when evaluated on the Hindi-English code-mixed language dataset, HINMIX. When compared to other cutting-edge models, our model demonstrates improved performance across eight distinct evaluation metrics. To validate the effectiveness of our data augmentation strategy, we also conducted ablation tests using non-code-mixed data for sentence classification tasks. These experiments confirmed our hypothesis that non-code-mixed data augmentation has a negative impact on model performance in code-mixed languages. To validate the accuracy of our transition point detection method, we employed human evaluation, where three independent assessors agreed on the identified transition points in code-mixed sentences between Hindi and English. Furthermore, we have made our model's pre-trained weights accessible, allowing for future research to leverage our model as a feature extractor for downstream NLP tasks. The average effect in Fisher's causal model is often overlooked, yet it holds crucial importance for determining the conditions under which an intervention can be expected to have a certain effect when applied to a specific individual. Fisher's own method for identifying these conditions, which involves examining the intersection of individual covariate-response functions, becomes problematic and difficult to define mathematically for cases with multiple covariates. In such scenarios, defining mean effect functions becomes essential, and they provide a viable alternative for analyzing these conditions. Furthermore, mean effect functions can be estimated more easily than Fisher's mean effect, and they offer valuable insights into how much an effect size can be expected to change following an intervention in a particular individual. We demonstrate that mean effect functions are essential for understanding the causal model known as Fisher's mean effect, and we outline the steps required for performing inference on these functions within the context of randomized controlled trials. In contrast to our novel findings, traditional inferential methods for Fisher's mean effect are shown to be ineffective and unreliable. Ultimately, mean effect functions provide a more comprehensive and informative understanding of Fisher's causal model, and they offer a valuable perspective on the conditions under which an intervention can be expected to have a certain effect when applied to a specific individual. In addition to these theoretical contributions, we also outline the steps required for implementing our proposed methods in the R programming language. We illustrate the utility of our methods through two real-world examples, and we highlight their potential applications in clinical trials. Future soldier wearables and robotic legged systems will greatly benefit from self-contained, portable power sources, such as miniature thrusters that utilize atmospheric gases and a specialized liquid fuel. By harnessing this potential, we investigate the feasibility of using these propulsion systems in bipedal gaits to produce comparable or improved outputs in terms of speed, stability, and productivity. Our research reveals that dynamic movements influenced by propulsion can outperform traditional walking techniques, which are restricted by leg length, when factors such as stride frequency, thrust duration, and foot placement are taken into consideration. Furthermore, we discovered that thrust-assisted walking can enhance stability through the application of external forces, thus reducing the need for high-powered and lengthy leg designs. Our findings indicate that bipedal locomotion facilitated by propulsion can be an effective strategy for enhancing efficiency and resilience. This research introduces a visual relocalization technique that utilizes 3D surfel maps. It combines geometric and photometric information from previously gathered data to pinpoint a robot's present location. Due to visual factors like weather conditions and shape changes, relocalization within a previously mapped area can be challenging without prior knowledge of the environment's geometry. Our approach leverages a trained deep neural network to extract image features, which are then compared with mapped images to achieve precise positioning. To optimize feature extraction, we developed a method for refining previously gathered data by aligning it with newly captured images. Additionally, our system enables a direct comparison of map and image features by incorporating geometric information into its feature learning process. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method yields more accurate results compared to state-of-the-art techniques that rely on keyframe localization within a 2D map. It achieves an average positioning error of 0.42m under real-world conditions, outperforming existing methods by over 0.2m. Our method has been successfully tested in a real-world environment and exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art techniques, with details available at https://tinyurl.com/surferlocalization. Our approach can be applied in a wide range of autonomous systems, including robots and drones, and is particularly suitable for environments where geometric patterns are scarce, such as indoor spaces and construction sites. It also offers improved efficiency and scalability over existing techniques, with direct and seamless integration into current localization methods. By leveraging geometric information from previously gathered data, our approach enables more accurate positioning at a lower computational cost. With continued advancements in deep neural networks and 3D mapping technology, our technique serves as a foundation for developing more sophisticated geometric-assisted visual localization methods in the future. Mobile devices are creating large datasets of image and signal data, which experts classify as having high or low values. Yet, different users have distinct definitions of what constitutes high or low values, leading to inconsistent labels. This problem is compounded when gadgets capture data under varying environmental conditions, resulting in ambiguous labels. This research presents a new technique, combining the concepts of customized and semi-supervised learning, to mitigate the effects of ambiguous labels. Our method utilizes a neural network to generate probability distributions for data classes, allowing it to efficiently process a large number of mobile data labels. We test our approach against other methods, using real-world data related to sleep monitoring and road conditions, and find that it significantly improves accuracy and reduces errors when dealing with a large number of mobile data labels. Additionally, it reduces training time and requires fewer parameters than other methods. This research presents a novel solution to the ambiguity problem in mobile data labels, and our source code is available at https://github.com/zheng-huang/CR-FSSL. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms other methods by improving the accuracy of classification tasks by up to 11% and reducing errors by up to 40%. Moreover, it reduces training time by up to 70% and the required parameters by up to 97%. This research presents a new technique, customized federated semi-supervised learning with ambiguity reduction, which efficiently processes a large number of mobile data labels with high ambiguity levels. This approach improves the accuracy of classification tasks, reduces errors, and efficiently trains neural networks with a minimal number of parameters. This research has the potential to significantly impact mobile data annotation, and its source code is available at https://github.com/zheng-huang/CR-FSSL. Simulating seconds-long mergers of black holes and neutron stars using advanced numerical models, researchers have studied the general-relativistic interaction of neutrino-baryon matter and electromagnetic fields. Extensive high-resolution simulations were conducted for various initial magnetic field configurations, strengths, and properties of neutron star matter, modeling the dynamics of magnetized accretion disks and jets from equatorial outflows. In collisions with minimal magnetic fields, a standard model of neutron star matter, and a short-lived merger phase, a stable disk forms around the black hole, emitting gravitational waves and powerful jets that shine brightly across the electromagnetic spectrum. As magnetic field strength increases, a smaller mass of matter stays behind the black hole, more energy goes into jets, and their structure becomes more complex, with significant effects observed for different initial magnetic field configurations and various models of neutron star matter, particularly when the merger occurs with magnetic fields aligned or opposed. In collisions with extremely strong magnetic fields, a bar-like mass distribution forms around the black hole, leading to altered jet properties and reduced electromagnetic radiation. This paper delves into measuring the speed at which a continuous-time Markov process converges to its stationary Q-process. We resolve a long-standing open issue by demonstrating that the Q-process is consistently reached under either local L1 convergence or local mean-square convergence. Furthermore, several examples are provided to illustrate the primary outcome, which can result in both slow and rapid approaches to equilibrium depending on the underlying Markov process. We also introduce an exploratory method to approximate the Q-process and examine the performance of this method in the context of a detailed biological model. Additionally, a related open problem is stated. The study is published under a Creative Commons license, allowing free reproduction and distribution of its content. The complete text can be accessed at arxiv.org/abs/2207.01740.
