Generating truly random numbers is crucial for numerous applications, yet current techniques have drawbacks such as performance limitations, increased complexity, and higher energy consumption. This paper presents a novel method to create random numbers by taking advantage of voltage reductions in dynamic random-access memories and explores its underlying physics through a mathematical analysis. By reducing the memory's supply voltage below its required threshold, read operations become unreliable, resulting in random data bits that can be used for randomness generation. This process is independent of external factors like thermal noise, making it more robust and resistant to environmental conditions. By utilizing under scaled voltages, the proposed technique can function without additional power consumption, aside from inevitable read refresh operations. This paper is open-source, with details available at https://github.com/ahmed-abdelkader/TuRAN/tree/main. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method, which is capable of producing 30 Mbps of genuine random data at a cost of 0.12 nJ per bit, utilizing a commercially available 40 nm SRAM chip. This production rate is significantly higher than existing approaches and is scalable to deep-submicron technologies. Furthermore, the generated random bits exhibit exceptional uniformity and a low auto-correlation value of 0.003, meeting the standards for high-security applications outlined in the NIST SP 800-22 standard. This randomness generation method can be easily integrated into existing systems, providing a rapid and energy-efficient solution for genuine random number production. With ongoing advancements in technology, the proposed technique is poised to generate random numbers at an increasingly rapid pace. At a 16 nm process node, the method is capable of producing 1.5 Gbps random data at 0.27 nJ per bit. This research has far-reaching implications for the development of highly secure cryptographic systems, enabling them to meet stringent randomness requirements even in the presence of limited environmental randomness. More importantly, this work bridges the gap between random number production and computing, allowing these two processes to be coupled more efficiently. This synergy could give rise to novel concepts such as randomness-driven computing and energy-efficient security systems. Ultimately, the proposed technique may pave the way for highly secure cryptography to become a ubiquitous and affordable component of every electronic device. With ongoing technological advancements, highly secure cryptography may become integral to existing products, ultimately transforming the landscape of random number production and cryptography as a whole. At a broader level, this research has the potential to revolutionize various applications by leveraging the inherent randomness in their underlying systems, thereby enhancing security, energy efficiency, and overall performance.

The research further establishes that these regularizers are highly effective and easily outdo more sophisticated methods for controlling representation complexity. Additionally, the study identifies key environmental factors, such as dataset characteristics, that interact with these built-in regularizers and facilitate generalization. This understanding enables the development of simple neural network designs that produce robust outcomes in a variety of scenarios. Moreover, the research provides insights into the creation of new learning algorithms centered around the control of representation complexity. The findings are supported by extensive experiments conducted on image classification, synthetic datasets, and the game of CartPole. Employing $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ data and utilizing the standard $B$ meson decay chain at LHCb, along with the $B_s^0\to \phi\mu^+\mu^-$ line shape from CMS, the coefficients can be calculated without input from other Wilson expansions, yielding $C_9=-4.2(3.8)$ and $C_{10}=1.0(3.1)$ in units of $10^{-3}$, with the estimates valid at the scale $Q\sim 2$ GeV. These estimates are based on average branching ratios for $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays at LHCb and CMS, with the results being nearly independent of several Wilson coefficients with large, well-constrained central values. The new approach is expected to facilitate frequent, in-loop re-evaluations of the $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ Wilson coefficients as new experimental data becomes available. The new approach is also applicable to other $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ observables and can be used with upcoming data from Belle II. Furthermore, the approach may be adapted for use with $B_s^0\to \phi\mu^+\mu^-$ data from LHCb. The field of Automated Essay Grading (AEG) in Education has seen significant advancements in recent years, thanks in part to transformer models like BERT. This study aims to improve the accuracy of AEG by employing data augmentation techniques in various forms to enhance the quality of input sentences provided by students. We investigate the efficacy of different data enhancement methods and assess their impact when combined with BERT and similar sequential models. Notably, our research discovers that both sentence shuffling and token deletion methods outperform other data enhancement techniques, while sequential models exhibit superior performance overall. Furthermore, we also examine the relevance of sentence shuffling as an inductive bias in AEG and propose a new metric called Shufflon Similarity Index (SSI), which gauges the similarity between original and shuffled sentences to gauge a student's understanding. We also present an open-source implementation of our approach, allowing other researchers to replicate our findings and build upon our work. Additionally, we have made available the enhanced dataset used in this study, known as the NEAR-EE Dataset, comprising 13K student essays on the topic of Near Earth Asteroids, which can serve as a resource for further research in AEG. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that data enhancement methods can significantly boost the accuracy of AEG models, while the SSI metric offers a fresh perspective on assessing a student's comprehension. Overall, this study contributes novel insights to the fields of AEG and Education, along with an open-source repository and a new dataset that can facilitate future research in Education Technology and Natural Language Processing. Recent research has uncovered a phenomenon called "in-context learning," which enables small tasks to be performed within the context of a larger input, without requiring any special symbols or parameters to be adjusted, all of which can be achieved through the clever manipulation of the input text itself. A key factor that determines the success of this approach is having access to high-quality training data, which includes examples of the desired output for various input prompts. In the absence of such data, certain models, which have been pre-trained on a diverse range of texts, can still perform well on these tasks, even when provided with limited amounts of supplementary training data.

In our study, we examined the impact of using different pre-trained datasets on the ability of models to learn in-context. We used a large-scale language model, which was made available to us through a public API, to test our hypotheses. Our results show that models pre-trained on a general knowledge base like Wikipedia are better equipped to handle tasks that require a deep understanding of the world, whereas those pre-trained on a vast corpus of text like the internet archive are more effective at tasks that involve a similar level of contextual understanding. On the other hand, models pre-trained on a dataset of customer reviews are better suited to tasks related to opinion expression. Our findings suggest that the origin of the pre-trained data has a significant impact on the ability of models to learn in-context. By integrating COR with a cutting-edge 3D reconstruction method based on semantic keypoint information, we have created a versatile system for predicting both the position and shape of objects from various viewpoints, thereby enabling more accurate object tracking and navigation in cluttered environments. Our approach has been successfully tested on three public datasets, with the results indicating a significant enhancement in overall performance and resilience to data imperfections. Furthermore, our method excels in predicting object volume and surface area, as well as in detecting potential collisions between objects. To facilitate further research, we have released a public dataset known as the Resilient Dataset for Category-level Object Reconstruction (R-COR), which comprises images with varied levels of semantic keypoint noise. Our long-term goal is to develop a vision system capable of adapting to changing environmental conditions and providing a reliable geometric understanding of objects, even when key feature data is incomplete or compromised. With the R-COR dataset serving as a benchmark for evaluating object representation robustness, our proposed method is poised to set a new standard for resilient object perception. When dealing with the Cauchy distribution, constructing intervals and squares for estimating parameters $\gamma$ and $\delta$ from sample data, enables us to determine the probability that these estimates vary within certain limits as the sample size increases, essentially providing us with a measure of uncertainty. Notably, this method can also be extended to the parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ of the standard Cauchy distribution, by treating them as equivalent to $\gamma$ and $\delta$ respectively. Our analysis reveals that, as the sample size $n$ approaches infinity, the probability that these estimates fall within the specified limits, converges to a value greater than zero, even as the probability bounds seemingly converge to zero, indicating asymptotic uncertainty. To verify the accuracy of our interval and square estimates, we employed simulation techniques, comparing them to traditional mean-based estimates, revealing that, for smaller sample sizes, mean-based estimates often provide tighter bounds and may be more suitable for practical use in such cases. Nonetheless, our results suggest that, as the sample size increases, the accuracy of both interval and square estimates improves, while the interval estimates appear to be more precise in this regard. Ultimately, our findings provide a theoretical foundation for the estimation of parameters in the Cauchy distribution and may contribute to related research in the field of heavy-tailed distributions. Additionally, our work may have implications for the estimation of parameters in related distributions such as the Pareto, Weibull, and $t$ distributions. A simulation example is also included to demonstrate the application of our interval and square estimates to real-world data, using observations of the surface height of a pool after throwing a stone into it. Interestingly, this data was found to be consistent with a mixture of two Cauchy distributions, each representing different stages of the splashing process. Our analysis also reveals that the parameter estimates for this mixture distribution exhibit significant variability, yet our interval and square estimates are capable of capturing this uncertainty. In contrast, traditional mean-based estimates fail to account for this uncertainty, revealing a notable limitation of this method in practice. Our work may have implications for the estimation of parameters in mixture distributions and highlights the importance of considering the underlying data generation process when conducting statistical analyses. A discussion of the relationship between our interval and square estimates and existing literature on the estimation of parameters in heavy-tailed distributions is also included. Our analysis reveals that these estimates are consistent with several established results in the field, thereby validating their accuracy. The goal of this research is to increase the efficiency and reliability of high-speed motion systems by using advanced linear parameter-varying (LPV) technology to enhance closed-loop performance and extend operational ranges. Traditional sequential loop closure methods are limited in their ability to achieve high precision due to variations in system parameters, but this study develops an LPV sequential closure algorithm that outperforms traditional methods, such as PID controls, in terms of precision and operational range. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulation and hardware testing of a high-accuracy motion system. The results show that the LPV sequential closure algorithm can achieve speeds up to 10 times faster and operational ranges up to 4 times longer compared to PID controls, while also providing more accurate and reliable motion performance. Furthermore, the LPV design was found to be easily implementable using widely available software tools, such as Simulink, which facilitated the transition from simulation to hardware testing. The LPV sequential closure algorithm was successfully applied in a real-world application, resulting in improved motion performance and expanded operational capabilities. The key findings of this study are expected to contribute to the development of more efficient, reliable, and high-accuracy motion systems in industries such as aerospace, automotive, and industrial automation. The proposed LPV sequential closure algorithm is also expected to have far-reaching applications in the control of complex dynamic systems with varying parameters. The research is a significant contribution to the field of systems and control theory, offering an innovative solution to the long-standing problem of achieving high precision and operational ranges in motion systems. We introduce a novel framework called PRNet, capable of partial-to-partial registration. This means aligning specific parts of one object with corresponding parts of another through a point-cloud representation. Our approach leverages deep learning to create a model that learns in a self-supervised manner, allowing it to capture complex geometric relationships within object points and generate a bijective mapping function. This bijective mapping is crucial for accurate one-to-one correspondence between point clouds. As a result, PRNet achieves improved robustness against partial visibility, even outperforming fully automatic methods like PoseCNN in some cases. We evaluate its effectiveness through a range of experiments, including comparisons with supervised learning techniques. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhkcos/PRNet. Specifically, our findings classify classes of groups that belong to $R_\infty$-characteristic, including those derived from fundamental groups of surfaces with additional symmetries and certain amalgamated free products. We also present an example illustrating that the $R_\infty$-characteristic does not encompass all groups with infinite cyclic commutator subgroups. The findings indicate that future high-energy electron-positron colliders such as CLIC or ILC offer the most efficient approach to investigate this topic, given their capacity to probe far-reaching energy scales with substantial sensitivity. In contrast, hadron colliders like the Future Circular Collider (FCC) or Large Hadron Collider (LHC) exhibit reduced sensitivity due to similar limitations and the presence of additional backgrounds. Ultimately, the optimal choice of collider depends on the specific goals and constraints of research into the Higgs and Standard Model effective field theory. The proposed research has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of quantum field theory at far-reaching energy scales. The analysis also highlights the significant advantages offered by circular e+e colliders over linear and circular proton colliders in probing this topic. A new method leveraging trajectory optimization is presented to extract key details from time-sensitive data, employing an iterative approach within a continuous framework rather than the traditional discrete least-squares method. This continuous framework is represented by a set of nonlinear equations that outline the event timeline. By treating uncertain parameters as variables to optimize and incorporating relevant constraints, the proposed method can accurately determine multiple parameters without excessive computational expense. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through applications to two real-world problems, including the determination of molecular spin lifetime and 24 nanometer asteroid shape, showcasing its capability to provide robust results even in the presence of noisy data. Furthermore, this method is shown to be relatively immune to initial guess inaccuracies. Due to its continuous nature, this method is named "sturdy inversion". It is anticipated that sturdy inversion will serve as a reliable technique for analyzing time-sensitive data across a range of scientific fields. A Python implementation of this method is available on the repository https://github.com/alexanderwarsinger/sturdy_inversion. Additionally, the corresponding capabilities have been integrated into the astrodynamics module of the flight Python package for the purpose of analyzing small asteroid shapes. This integration is available at https://flight-python.github.io/flight.html#astrodynamics. Furthermore, we investigate how the distribution amplitude for the $D^*_s$ meson is influenced by a strange quark. Predicting the next action in a sequence is crucial for understanding sequence data, which includes applications such as gesture recognition and speech forecasting. Current models, including RNNs and RLFMs, have achieved success but still struggle with capturing complex inter-task relationships, resulting in poor performance when multiple tasks are intertwined. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Feature Mapping RNN with a Radial Basis Function (FM-RBF). This model leverages a key function to transform sequence data into a more task-friendly feature space, where it uses an RNN to forecast future action probabilities. When applied to kitchen task forecasting, FM-RBF outperforms RNNs and state-of-the-art RLFMs, demonstrating the model's effectiveness. Additionally, we show that task diversity enhances forecasting performance, leading to improved results when applied to more challenging datasets. This research was inspired by prior work on action forecasting, and our findings are consistent with these findings. FM-RBF's source code is available at https://github.com/alexlee2000google/fm_rbf. FM-RBF has been registered as R2.2.0 on MAML.

Recent research on the $p$-core $p'$-configurations has yielded significant insights into the field. Notably, D. Livingstone's and R. L. Thomas's studies on alternating permutations align with the structure of these configurations, while M. El-Chaazly, A. H. Horozewski, and M. A. Morley discovered a connection between the duals of these configurations and the hypercube graph. In contrast, the nature of the obtained permutations that miss the $p$-core property remains unclear. In this research, we aim to address this question by investigating the properties of a random sample of these permutations within the scope of the additive residue graph. Our findings indicate that when the size of the permutations increases, the proportion of those that miss the $p$-core property converges to a value greater than 0.5, while exhibiting significant fluctuations in the intermediate range. Our results are further supported by numerical simulations, thus providing a practical understanding of the previously elusive aspect of the $p$-core $p'$-configurations. Moreover, our study offers a simplified explanation for the sign patterns observed in the LLT polytopes, as sign-reversing permutations, as reported by P. Chaudhuri, A. M. Cohen, and H. S. M. Coxeter. Our work also explores the distribution of the distance between two randomly selected vertices in the additive residue graph and presents an alternative proof of a theorem by A. G. Liddar and M. A. Morley concerning the existence of large cliques within this graph. Our research also reveals additional combinatorial structure in the duals of the $p$-core $p'$-configurations, as demonstrated by the presence of near-cliques and the efficient solvability of the clique problem in this graph. Furthermore, our study offers an efficient algorithm to generate the $p$-core $p'$-configurations and their duals up to a certain size and provides a computational exploration of the obtained permutations. This research explores an important issue in computational complexity, specifically how to identify the roots of a polynomial, given multiple evaluations of its output. With this new capability, we establish lower bounds on how efficiently polynomials can be solved, specifically quadratic and cubic equations, which surprisingly reveal that these lower bounds are more stringent when allowing for occasional errors compared to when the algorithm operates without errors. This work presents a novel method that allows the temporal gauge to influence the spatial metric's evolution, thereby ensuring various spatial metric derivative continuities. Utilizing the Conformal Transverse Traceless technique, we develop a strategy to create meanfields that can eliminate discontinuities and guarantee continuity of spatial metric derivatives during evolution. This employs a Fourier-space calculation for the meanfields' coefficients, which may lead to minor frequency-related amplification. However, our findings demonstrate that even with minor frequency amplification, the resulting spatial metric continuities can still be maintained without additional measures. This is particularly evident in our findings, where we show that ensuring the 1st and 2nd spatial derivatives of the spatial metric are continuous suffices to guarantee continuity of the 3rd and 4th spatial metric derivatives. Recently, pre-trained models have greatly simplified the data labeling process by generating labels that human annotators can then review. However, applying these models leads to another issue: the large number of models required for optimal results contributes to computational costs during training being excessively high. To resolve this problem, our research proposes a technique that learns from multiple models simultaneously by mimicking a human annotator's quality control process. Our approach leverages the differences between the output logits of these models to effectively aggregate the information and provide high-quality labels. Through experiments, we have demonstrated the capabilities of our method, particularly in the context of data annotation, where it surpasses the performance of individual models and even that of human annotators with or without prior knowledge. Through this technique, we've demonstrated the capability to decrease the predicted lower limits on the elastic scattering cross-section by at least one order of magnitude across a wide range of mass values, from picograms to femtograms. Even in cases where the method's signal enhancement is relatively small, a significant reduction in cross-section limits is still achievable with modest system design enhancements. We've also applied strength interferometry to experimental data from XENON10 and XENON100 dark matter detection experiments, resulting in slightly tighter constraints on the elastic scattering cross-section. This paper explores the process of basis pursuit in the context of continuous spaces, with a focus on its output's uniqueness. It is demonstrated that, even with a continuous space and an arbitrarily small error tolerance, basis pursuit may not produce a singular solution. Additionally, under specific conditions, the number of non-unique solutions can be quantified. The study also identifies particular situations in which baseline methods like the limited memory BFGS algorithm and soft thresholding provide a single solution, with or without augmentation. A graphical illustration, incorporating the Riemannian manifold structure of sparse solutions, sheds light on the issue from a geometric perspective. This allows the introduction of a novel concept, denoted 'rigidity', to describe solution sets' topological characteristics. It is then established that augmenting certain methods with continuous optimization tools enhances their 'rigidity' and, consequently, their ability to deliver a singular solution. The theoretical findings are substantiated through numerous numerical experiments. The research also presents an open question, along with suggested possible answers. Network administrators face difficulties in translating policy changes into hardware due to the resource-intensive process and inflexible programmable components on current routers. As a result, many network devices still rely on traditional routers for specific policies, which limits their efficiency. A new approach, the P416 compiler, translates policy specifications into configurable match-action rules that can be easily implemented on programmable switches, bypassing expensive hardware updates. Our research builds on previous studies and expands the P416 compiler's capabilities to support more complex policies, including policies with missing or alternative action elements. Additionally, we created an open-source P416 compiler framework that facilitates compilation of real-world policies and compares its results to other methods with our experimental findings. Overall, our findings show that the P416 compiler can efficiently reduce the number of rules needed to implement policies compared to other methods, while also providing a flexible solution for programmable switches and a feasible approach for updating policy changes in hardware. The open-source P416 compiler framework is available at https://github.com/CompNet/P416_Compiler. Further details on our experimental setup and additional results can be found at https://compnet.cs.nyu.edu/P416_Compiler. It is proven that the enhanced method retains second-order accuracy in L2 norm, while significantly improving ehrlich's estimate, thereby yielding a more precise local estimate that is comparable to the initial RT0 scheme up to machine precision when applied to smooth vector fields. To achieve this, two main strategies are employed: initially, a conforming interpolant is constructed, based on a reference solution that satisfies an amended equation; subsequently, an iterative process is employed to refine the estimate through successive solution corrections. Furthermore, it is shown that the method can be modified to accommodate non-conforming RT0 elements, enabling its application in coarser schemes through a novel duality-based approach. Consequently, the method can be utilized on a diverse range of quadrilateral meshes without undergoing a mesh refinement process. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The growing popularity of federated learning can be attributed to its ability to balance data protection and performance, enabling collaborations among institutions with disparate data collections. Nonetheless, research has uncovered hidden disparities within horizontally structured FL datasets, which are produced by similar data sources but varying demographic groups. This study delves into the intersection of FL and fairness, examining how fairness metrics are affected by the federalistic nature of FL. We also explore the connection between privacy and fairness within FL, utilizing the Recurrent Neural Networks as a benchmark to evaluate the impact of privacy on demographic groups and fairness. Our results indicate that boosting Recurrent Neural Networks using stochastic gradient descent leads to improved accuracy at the expense of fairness, with demographic group affinities exacerbating this trade-off, especially for groups with smaller data collections, and regardless of the employed regularization methods. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical link between differential privacy and fairness, revealing that differential privacy can mitigate demographic group biases but may introduce new biases in certain scenarios. Based on these findings, we suggest several strategies to balance performance, fairness, and privacy in FL. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexandroschamering/fedlearn_equity_dp.

Human action understanding in video has been effectively achieved through deep learning techniques, but current methods still face challenges such as inaccurate action part identification. This issue is addressed in our research by proposing the Hierarchical Focus Network (HFN), a model that not only accurately identifies overall actions but also their corresponding parts. To achieve this, we designed HFN with two interconnected components - a Hierarchical Focus Module (HFModule) and a Focus Feature Fusion (F3) Module. The first module enables the selection of relevant frames for overall action identification and part recognition through a combination of focus filters, while the second module integrates features from focused frames to produce part-aware representations. To train the model effectively, we developed a multi-task loss function that optimizes overall action identification and part recognition performance simultaneously. Evaluation of HFN on the UT-Interaction and JHMDB-21 datasets reveals its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of mean average precision (MAP) scores, underscoring its ability to improve action part identification through focused frame selection. Furthermore, the proposed model's trained focus filters can be leveraged to generate new focus filters for unseen actions, demonstrating its general applicability. To validate this, we conducted a supplementary experiment where we employed the trained HFModule to select focused frames for novel actions not seen during training, and found that overall action identification accuracy remained high even with reduced frames. Increasingly, optimization methods are being used to uncover a broad range of solutions, but current assessment techniques are not well-suited for this purpose. As a result, the potential of multi-objective optimization (MOO) and quality diversity (QD) is often going to waste. To address this, we introduce a new evaluation framework that provides a clear understanding of a solution's diversity and its relationship to the dimensions of the problem. Using this framework, we are able to demonstrate that many optimization methods are not as effective at promoting diversity as previously thought and that current approaches actually encourage convergence on a single optimum. To rectify this issue, we present two new algorithms that effectively increase diversity and enable the discovery of more phenotypic variety. The first, Phenotype Manipulator, introduces variety by mapping different solutions to alternative phenotypes, while the second, Genotype Phenotype Diversity, encourages variety by incorporating the cost of the genotype-phenotype mapping process into the optimization objective. When tested on a range of real-world problems, our proposed methods outperformed existing solutions and enabled the discovery of numerous solution phenotypes. This research introduces reinforcement learning as a technique to create quantum gate error correction codes capable of withstanding arbitrary quantum noise. Traditional approaches relying on repeated gate experiments to establish correction strategies are insufficient due to their exposure and vulnerability. In contrast, our method enables learning these protocols in a quantum-black-box manner, where input parameters are passed through the black box to obtain an output, without necessitating repeated experimentation. We present two implementations of reinforcement learning coders for fault-resilient quantum computation, the first based on neural networks and the second on policy-based learning, and demonstrate their efficiency in protecting quantum information against arbitrary noise by consistently achieving high rewards. Furthermore, we outline the benefits of transferring this approach to existing quantum algorithms, which could lead to substantial gains in computation reliability. We anticipate our contribution to spark the development of more robust quantum computing systems. The CLICTD experiment, set up at the Isracool's PIETRA laboratory in Italy, is designed to test the feasibility of using LAr-based detectors in nuclear and particle physics research. This R&D project focuses on developing double-phase active and passive detection systems with integrated electronics. This paper examines the properties of various sensing crystal options, evaluating their performance based on light output, ionization yield, thermal properties, and radioactivity levels. The study reveals that the best option features a 5 cm long and 10 cm wide collection electrode, coupled with a 5 cm thick sensing module composed of a 5 x 5 x 6 cm PWO crystal. The results also suggest that the choice of monocrystalline substrate has a minimal impact on detector properties. However, further optimization is required to optimize performance across the entire active volume of the CLICTD detector. Additionally, using poly-crystalline substrates could offer a cost-effective solution without compromising functionality. Future work will focus on refining the design and testing different sensing crystal orientations to achieve uniform response and highest possible light output across the collection electrode. Finally, the team will select the best technology option for large-scale LAr detector projects moving forward. Time-resolved beta-source testing and final optimization are scheduled for the autumn of this year at Isracool's PIETRA laboratory. When conducting a meta-analysis with paired data points from the same study, such as correlated means, our method builds upon previous work by providing a more straightforward and efficient way to estimate parameters. This involves extending the concepts of "sturdy" estimators, originally developed for individual study data, to the level of studies, with improved performance even when individual data is poorly estimated. Typically, collision models in fluid simulations rely on a specific time frame, often derived from the material's relaxation time, to determine when a collision has occurred. However, this approach can result in an unrealistic collision duration when simulating individual particles, mainly due to the varying distances between particles. To address this limitation, a novel multi-time-step integration method has been developed, allowing for the use of different time frames for particle collisions and fluid simulation calculations. The method utilizes particle positions from lower-time-step simulations as virtual particles to determine when a collision has occurred based on a specified threshold, rather than solely relying on the fluid simulation's time frame. As a result, this method enables collision detection that is not skewed by spacing and improves overall simulation accuracy. Additionally, when combined with adaptive techniques for updating particle positions, this method can accelerate collision detection while maintaining precise results. The results show that this method successfully reduces spacing-related errors in collision detection and can significantly lower computational costs by preventing unnecessary and close interactions between particles. The method has also demonstrated its ability to accurately model high-speed collisions between particles. Investigating the source of radiation energy is crucial in understanding the Unruh/Hawking phenomenon. When considering particle number, the virtual pair's creation and annihilation process near the event horizon appears to be the source of real particles. However, examining the momentum distribution of these particles reveals that they originate from the emitter/observer, not the particle pairs. The emission is actually a nonlocal process resulting from the EPR entanglement, formed during the annihilation of the virtual pair. The event horizon acts as a local indicator of the EPR correlation's dissolution, which causes the momentum redistribution. The Unruh/Hawking phenomenon can be reinterpreted as a specific manifestation of quantum entanglement leading to radiation. The proposed mechanism is applicable not only to black holes but also to other situations, such as the zero-temperature Draperon hole and the laser-scattered particle hole. The derived emission spectra for these cases are in line with the existing literature. The method employed here can serve as a general approach to understand the local signs of EPR entanglement-related phenomena. The approach can be applied to the anti-particle side of the Unruh/Hawking phenomenon as well. The analysis offers a clear, local understanding of the Unruh/Hawking phenomenon, which should facilitate its experimental verification. The analysis also sheds light on the dual nature of the event horizon, which is a fundamental aspect of quantum field theory in the Dodelson-Lukyanov representation. The analysis provides a new perspective on the measurement process, which is often considered as a one-way event. The analysis reveals that the event horizon is not only a passive observer but also an active participant in the measurement process. We conducted a comprehensive study to evaluate the flux-based statistical forecast initially proposed by Quast and Eisenstein. The theory posits that the evolution of chaotic systems can be accurately predicted over the long term by following the flow of initial conditions within their phase space. Our investigation specifically examines how this forecasting method handles the three-body problem, specifically using the widely analyzed case of the binary-nebula system. By comparing the predicted orbital periods to those observed in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 16, we found a notable discrepancy of about an order of magnitude. Furthermore, the distribution of predicted binary system ages appears to shift towards younger values, which contradicts the observed trends in the SDSS dataset. The possibility of resolving these discrepancies through future surveys capable of detecting tighter binary systems is also explored. The theoretical framework behind the flux-based forecasting method may hold significant value in understanding the hard binary populations that are difficult to analyze using N-body simulations. However, addressing the associated computational challenges will be essential to leveraging this approach effectively. The proposed structure comprises four key layers: the domain of formulas, their semantics, axioms, and an algebraic category representing Boolean algebras with continuous operations. We demonstrate that this category maintains the properties of a complete and compact algebraic category, enabling representation theorems that reflect the category-theoretic characteristics of model theory. Furthermore, we define continuous versions of Turing categories and computability, establishing that continuous computability is universally equivalent to static computability. We apply this framework to examine the complexity classes $\mathsf{P}$ and $\mathsf{NP}$ within continuous computability, and derive a corresponding computability-theoretic consequence. This work introduces a novel method to represent and study the interfaces between gas and liquid phases in two-dimensional flows using skeletal data structures. By leveraging the principles of Voronoi diagrams and Delaunay triangulations, we generate skeletons in real-time, allowing for their computation during online analysis. A graph representation, denoted as $\mathcal{G}$, is utilized to store skeleton information, which encompasses the interplay between branch points (vertices) and segments (edges). A quantitative measure, branch point importance, is defined and used to prioritize vertices during reduction operations, resulting in a simplified representation of the interface. This method enhances online analysis capabilities by providing a compact representation of the interface and enabling calculations with reduced complexity. It is demonstrated that the proposed approach outperforms traditional interface representations in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy, as evidenced by its ability to accurately track the interface area and gross error for various flow types, even at high speeds. Furthermore, the method enables the computation of the Stokes stress tensor and the Reynolds stress tensor at specified points, as shown in the presented results. A Python package, pySkeleton, is developed to implement this method and is made available for public use. The method's efficacy is validated through experiments on three multi-phase flow types: a single bubble rising due to surface tension, a collision between two droplets, and a periodic flow with oscillating bubbles. The detailed implementation and analysis of this method can be found in the accompanying open-source repository at https://github.com/NeSTMLG/pySkeleton. A Jupyter notebook is also provided for online visualization at https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/gist/ahmedebrahim/7a5f0b8c0c0e4b5c5a0c0100c. Research has uncovered a novel phenomenon where viruses autonomously roll themselves into ordered structures upon adhering to a surface, primarily driven by the contraction of associated protein capsids. The underlying physics governing this self-rolling process appears to be contingent on the surface's chemical properties rather than the virus's inherent characteristics. In this investigation, we employ three-dimensional simulations to model rolling surfaces comprising different types of viruses and examine how various surface properties impact the rolling dynamics. Furthermore, we validate our model against experimental data and analyze the underlying physics to identify potential applications for self-assembling viral structures. Additionally, we explore the possibility of controlling viral movement through external stimuli. This frequency range, where the impact is most significant, is surprisingly close to the inverse of the chaotic oscillation frequency in the unmodified system. Our research demonstrates that time lag modulation can produce substantial amplification in chaotic systems, offering potential applications in various fields, such as biology and medicine. It also highlights a critical limitation of numerical simulations that typically model time delays without accounting for their potential modulation, which can lead to misleading conclusions about system dynamics, particularly at high frequencies. Therefore, we recommend using delays with boundaries or other forms of representation that naturally incorporate the possibility of modulation. If such representations are not used, we provide guidance on how to interpret the results in terms of actual system behavior when delays in natural systems are modulated, as in the case of external interventions. Finally, we illustrate the practical relevance of our findings through two examples, one involving the control of neural seizures and the other the regulation of population growth. Imitation learning seeks to obtain a robot's behavior by mimicking a demonstrated action, but its effectiveness is constrained when demonstrations are scarce, infrequently recorded, or specific to particular tasks, due to the challenge of generalizing across variations. When imitation learning data is limited to observations rather than executable actions, the problem becomes even more complex because the robot's state space is not fully observable. This research presents a novel approach that combines both issues, allowing a robot to imitate behaviors in diverse areas using incomplete observations and specific demonstrations. The method employs a variational autoencoder to produce usable states from observations and constructs a shared latent space across domains by integrating both state and action information. Through experiments in multiple simulation environments, the proposed framework demonstrates the ability to mimic various tasks in different settings using only a single demonstration in real-world state space. The results show that this approach outperforms existing methods by a significant margin. A video showcasing the method's capabilities is available at https://youtu.be/6Q8xk0QxkxU. This research investigates how court-ordered mental health treatment affects the behavior of convicted individuals, focusing on those exhibiting no obvious mental health issues. Using a proprietary consumer database and a panel of individuals convicted between 2003 and 2013 in eight US states, we examine the impact of mandated therapy. Our findings reveal that those required to undergo treatment show a 7-10% decrease in violent crimes and a 5-6% decrease in property crimes within a two-year period following their conviction. Interestingly, the benefits of treatment are more pronounced when judges personally mandate the therapy, indicating that being held accountable by a higher authority enhances the treatment's effectiveness. Notably, the positive outcomes of treatment are more significant for individuals who are younger, non-white, and have a history of criminal activity. Ultimately, our study suggests that court-ordered mental health treatment can reduce recidivism rates, underscoring the potential for the criminal justice system to promote positive social outcomes. Given the low costs associated with this intervention, our research highlights a compelling example of how the criminal justice system can encourage individual improvement and community well-being. Based on our estimates, the estimated annual savings from reduced crimes in the study sample exceeds $210 million, with potential broader applications if similar results are observed in other cohorts. To further explore this hypothesis, our analysis will be supplemented by a second paper that examines a cohort of individuals convicted between 2013 and 2017. By comparing the outcomes of two treatment groups and one control group, our research will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the impact of court-ordered mental health treatment on convicted individuals. Ultimately, our findings will shed light on the complex interplay between the criminal justice system and individual mental health issues. Given the low costs associated with this intervention, our research highlights a compelling example of how the criminal justice system can encourage individual improvement and promote positive social outcomes. With bipartisan support for diversion programs that redirect offenders into community-based treatment, our research offers a timely perspective on the effectiveness of such initiatives. By examining the impact of court-ordered mental health treatment, our research seeks to inform policy discussions surrounding these programs and their potential to modify the behavior of convicted individuals. By leveraging our analysis, judges can make more informed decisions when imposing sentences, and policymakers can assess the efficacy of mental health treatment as a means to reduce recidivism rates. This research introduces an innovative method for detecting anomalies in time-series data by analyzing how well hidden markov models (HMMs) fit the data. The traditional approach to anomaly detection using HMMs focuses on models that are already trained and how well new data matches them. In contrast, our approach involves modifying this process to identify anomalies within these trained models by evaluating the probability of observed data given the HMM states. To achieve this, we replace the standard forward algorithm used in HMM analysis with a gauge-like transformation, which enables us to compare the behavior of non-anomalous and anomalous data points within the same model. By applying this change, we can quantify anomalies based on their deviation from the predicted gauge probability. This method was successfully tested on real-world time-series datasets related to machinery and stock market activity. Furthermore, our approach was compared to established anomaly detection methods using support vector machines (SVMs) and one-class SVMs, with the results demonstrating its effectiveness. With its ability to detect anomalies within non-anomalous data sequences and its ability to handle sequences of varying lengths, our method outperforms the SVM-based methods in certain scenarios. The source code for this research is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/alexander-schulz/anomaly_detection_hmm. Additionally, a pre-trained HMM model used in this study can be accessed through our dedicated webpage: https://hmm-anomaly-identification.herokuapp.com. This platform also includes interactive visualizations and examples of anomaly detection in real-time series data. By clicking on the 'Detect Anomalies' button, users can upload their own data and view the results, which include the predicted anomalies and the predicted gauge probability for each data point. This allows users to further explore and refine their understanding of the data and its underlying HMM model. With its ability to detect anomalies within trained HMM models, our approach offers an innovative solution to a previously overlooked problem in anomaly detection. Furthermore, its ability to handle sequences of varying lengths and its ability to detect anomalies even when they deviate slightly from the normal behavior, sets it apart from other methods. Current research on data enhancement has primarily focused on creating training datasets from existing information, but these methods often demand considerable effort from users. In contrast, we propose a novel form of data enhancement that identifies underutilized knowledge in users and efficiently incorporates it into speech data. To achieve this, we have developed an automatic technique for identifying acoustic cues related to specific words or phrases. This technique not only enhances the quality of speech data but also provides additional semantic information, thereby boosting both speech and text translation models. Our test findings indicate that this method results in improved translation accuracy and reduced translation errors, with an approximate 7% decrease in total translation error rate compared to standard baseline models. Crucially, this method can be applied without modifying its underlying architecture to other types of sequential data. Our source code and demo are available for public access at https://github.com/knownspace/MEDE.

A significant gap exists in the current theoretical guarantees when applying the Laplace mechanism to obtain safe sums. This research presents a novel method to reduce this disparity by introducing an influence measure that helps establish precise confidentiality breach thresholds. Additionally, the research introduces specific methods to create confidential cumulative distribution function releases while formulating a dependency-based privacy measure and developing an optimization technique to control confidentiality breaches under various dependency types. Finally, an experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed methods in maintaining confidentiality with minimal personalization constraints. With significant potential applications in high-stakes personalization settings, such as medical treatment, this research offers a new approach to balancing personalization and confidentiality. The goal of Visual Inconsistency Detection, which analyzes image alterations, has significant real-world implications and has proven beneficial in various applications such as product rating and visual merchandising. Although the field has been researched extensively, there remains a need to address its core challenges, including accurately detecting both minor and substantial changes across both internal and external modifications. In this paper, a novel approach called VICTOR is introduced, which leverages a dual transformer architecture that combines benefits from local and global feature analysis. Notably, by employing a pre-trained model tailored to the fashion industry through a contrastive learning approach, the model is enabled to effectively grasp transformation patterns and make predictions more efficiently. As evidence of its effectiveness, VICTOR achieves remarkable performance on the Fashionista dataset, surpassing current best models by a substantial margin of 10.0% in F1 score. Furthermore, the source code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to facilitate future research and development in this area. Additionally, a public demo of this work can be accessed here: https://victor-visual-inconsistency-detector.technologent.com/.

To address this, researchers have developed asynchronous and buffered aggregation techniques, but they still require users to wait for the next available communication slot, reducing efficiency. Temporal knowledge graphs exhibit significant potential in various applications such as traffic forecasting and stock market predictions due to their ability to model real-world events with temporal connections. Nevertheless, accurately predicting future relationships (link forecasting) in these graphs remains a difficult task. The widespread adoption of deep learning frameworks has led to the creation of numerous trainable models, but some link forecasting methods still rely on traditional techniques or special-purpose models that require extensive training time. In this research, we demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing pre-trained deep learning models for link forecasting by treating the task as a classification problem. Furthermore, we highlight the benefits of employing static models, which can provide quick and accurate predictions even in large graph datasets. Our experimental findings showcase the effectiveness of static models in link forecasting, and we compare their performance against specialized models and an approach that integrates static and dynamic components. The code and knowledge graph datasets used in this study are available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Our results show that static models can serve as efficient and accurate solutions for link forecasting, particularly when datasets are small or model retraining is not feasible due to computational constraints. Additionally, static models can function as short-term predictors, and their combination with dynamic models could potentially yield even better results. Our findings also suggest that static models tend to excel at predicting relationships with established patterns, whereas dynamic models may perform better with less frequent or more volatile relationships. Lastly, static models can provide substantial speed-ups (up to 3 orders of magnitude) in inference time, making them more suitable for real-time applications where rapid model predictions are essential. In summary, our research indicates that static models offer a convenient, efficient, and effective solution for link forecasting, and their integration with dynamic models could lead to even more accurate predictions. Our work also sheds light on the characteristics of relationships that static models and dynamic models tend to predict, which could facilitate further research in this area. Two infinite path-finite graph edges can be considered equivalent if there's a homeomorphism preserving directions, sending one edge to another. It demonstrates that every robust shift equivalent class contains a graph with only one non-trivial vertex and connects this concept to Cuntz-Hout representation stability, revealing a relationship between robust shift equivalence and a specific stability condition. Additionally, the authors present three open questions related to robust shift equivalence. Furthermore, the paper links robust shift equivalence to the K-theory of the C*-algebra, and through it, to the homotopy type of its boundary algebra, leading to a conjecture about the latter's invariance under homotopy equivalence. Finally, the paper presents a method to compute the tensor product of two C*-algebras' K-theory based on the graphs representing the algebras, and it uses this computation to derive invariants from the graphs, including the topological K-theory of the algebras. These invariants are shown to be robust shift equivalence invariants. The paper concludes by connecting these invariants to the Cuntz-Hout stability condition and the Morita stable isomorphism type of the algebras. The authors also present four open questions related to these invariants. The methods employed in the paper draw from diverse mathematical fields including topology, combinatorics, homological algebra, C*-algebra theory, noncommutative geometry, and homological stability. Our research investigates how Hausdorff measure behaves in the quasiregular dynamical context, providing both generalising and contrasting outcomes in comparison to the holomorphic setting. Specifically, we've identified scenarios in which the Hausdorff dimension of a quasiregular self-map on $\mathbb{C}$ either increases, remains constant, or decreases given an arbitrary initial measure. Additionally, we've discovered that, in sharp contrast to the holomorphic case, Hausdorff measure is not uniquely determined by the dimension and potential of a quasiregular self-map, even when constrained to $\mathbb{C}$. Furthermore, we've found new applications of Wold's decomposition in the context of quasiregular maps defined over one-dimensional manifolds. Lastly, we've established an intriguing connection between Hausdorff measure and the Lyapunov exponent in the context of one-dimensional quasiregular maps with finitely many attractants. Specifically, we've found that the Lyapunov exponent is zero and the Hausdorff measure of the attractors is zero if the map has positive combinatorial entropy, while the Lyapunov exponent is positive and the Hausdorff measure of the attractors is positive if the map has negative combinatorial entropy. Conversely, we've found a counterexample to the hypothesis that positive Lyapunov exponent implies finite non-zero Hausdorff measure of attractors in one-dimensional quasiregular maps defined over $\mathbb{C}$. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons and nuclear vectors, known as ultraperipheral collisions. This research focuses on the latter, specifically examining the production of J/ψ forward photons in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at a center of mass energy of 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector. Our analysis involved incorporating recently upgraded electron-positron reconstruction techniques, yielding the first measurement of J/ψ forward production at rapidities between -3.6 and -4.3 and at forward transverse momenta below 15 GeV/$^2$ between 2.5 and 3.5. This improvement in detection also allowed for the investigation of nuclear vector modifications in the vector mesons, specifically through the examination of their $z$-dependence, which compares the relative suppression of J/ψ forward production at various $z$ values in central and peripheral Pb--Pb collisions. Additionally, we present findings on the coherent photoproduction of J/ψ on individual nucleons within the target, utilizing an advanced analysis and incorporating data from both lead-lead and proton-lead collisions, which serve as reference targets. This research contributes to our understanding of nuclear vector modifications in the context of nuclear scale photoproduction and sheds light on the production mechanisms involved. Lastly, we compare our measured J/ψ production suppression at a rapidity of -3.6 to model predictions, which are primarily based on the Glauber and EPSHE formalisms. This comparison also includes the consideration of cold nuclear matter effects, which are analyzed using the SAL and URQMD generators. This comparison aims to deepen our comprehension of nuclear vector modifications and the interplay of multiple effects in ultraperipheral collisions. This research introduces a novel technique known as Controllable Soundpainting, which enables the creation of sound through visual stimuli, allowing artists to explore the intersection of visuals and audio in an interactive dance. The Synestheme System, our proposed method, utilizes the effects of synaesthesia and spatial resampling to generate unique sounds from visually perceived frequencies and timbre characteristics. The Synestheme Editor application enables artists to craft and manipulate soundpaints using a combination of visual and auditory inputs, ultimately leading to a dynamic and immersive experience that correlates visuals with sound. The resulting soundpaints are not only influenced by the visual stimuli but also controlled in real-time by the user's auditory feedback, offering an unprecedented level of artistic expression and creativity. Our findings are demonstrated through an interactive video showcasing the soundpainting process and a set of 200 manually created soundpaints serving as a reference dataset for further development. The Synestheme System's source code and soundpaints dataset are available for public use at https://github.com/keungrakp/. The success of data-driven applications relies heavily on the quality of their underlying data. However, ensuring data quality is a challenging task, particularly during the early stages of a project when data availability and volume are relatively low. To address this issue, a novel approach called data troubleshooting is proposed, which applies the Shapley value concept to end-to-end machine learning pipelines. Each data asset is paired with a machine learning task it supports, and then undergoes evaluation to determine its impact on a specific outcome. This process enables data managers to identify the data assets that have the greatest impact on each task, as well as allocate resources more efficiently. To effectively evaluate data assets, a general framework called DataShap is introduced, which can calculate their value contribution for a wide range of applications without requiring prior knowledge. DataShap relies on Monte Carlo sampling methods and can be applied to various data assets, machine learning algorithms, and tasks, as well as custom models, making it a versatile tool. The approach was successfully validated using real-world datasets and custom machine learning models to demonstrate its effectiveness in assessing data assets and assigning importance levels. This was achieved by integrating the system into a data management system, allowing it to analyze multiple data assets and tasks, as well as providing a comprehensive understanding of their value contribution. Furthermore, the approach offers several benefits, including improved decision-making, optimized resource allocation, and enhanced data asset management. To showcase its capabilities, data troubleshooting was applied to two practical case studies, highlighting its ability to assign importance levels to data assets and demonstrate its effectiveness in a real-world context. Based on these findings, the paper concludes that data troubleshooting is a valuable tool for data management and provides a potential solution for improving data quality. hypergraph reconstruction (GHR) approach is proposed, aiming to restore missing
connections between objects of interest through an existing framework, such as a
standard hypergraph-based image segmentation method. This is achieved by first
capturing the main objects' characteristics within individual regions of interest
using a kernel-based process, then using these characteristics to recreate the
original high-level image structure and interaction between objects before
enforcing the original labels on the resulting reconstruction through a constraint
process. This novel GHR method can serve as an essential component in other more
complex frameworks to enhance the robustness of overall framework in object-based
image analysis. The benefits and effectiveness of the proposed GHR approach are

To facilitate advancements in chest X-ray analysis, we have created and made public a large dataset of 29,376 images along with their annotations. Building on existing knowledge in the field, we've developed detailed, multi-scale annotations for each image, starting with an overview of the patient's condition and then moving on to specific findings such as abnormalities, lesions, or injuries, all of which are linked through a hierarchical structure. Our approach differs from traditional annotation methods in that we use CT projections to accurately represent the location and density of findings on two-dimensional X-ray images. This method allows us to accurately represent the presence of multiple findings in the same region. We plan to make our dataset publicly available under a permissive license to support future research. We believe that by sharing this dataset, it will enable researchers to gain a deeper understanding of the complexities involved in multi-finding localization and to develop more comprehensive diagnostic systems for automated analysis. Additionally, we have launched a new benchmark for evaluating the accuracy of multiple finding detection and localization in chest X-rays, which can be accessed at our website. This benchmark currently includes two tasks: identifying the overall condition of the patient and locating specific findings. We anticipate that as more datasets become available, we will continue to refine our annotation guidelines to align with the evolving standards in the medical field. Furthermore, we reveal that there is a connection between the entropic gauge and Srinivasan-Lakshminarayanan complexity measures, which offers additional insight into emission properties. Our study provides a simple and useful tool for exploring microcavity laser design and optimizing directional emission. Ultimately, this research has the potential to contribute to the development of novel integrated photonics applications. We analyzed data from the Magnetometer and Fast Plasma Investigation instruments on board the MMS spacecraft for its M1 and M2 flybys near the Sun. This data revealed various plasma waves including their combinations within the solar corona and interplanetary medium, spanning a distance of 0.13 to 0.8 solar radii from the Sun's surface. Observations inside the corona detected the solar breeze at speeds of about 20 km/s and identified a source of whistler mode waves linked to the ion acoustic instability. Additionally, we found that the solar wind's density and temperature varied significantly with altitude and were influenced by the background magnetic field strength. Outside the corona, we detected the most intense whistler mode waves at 0.5 solar radii and noted their association with the growing ion acoustic instability. This led to the conclusion that the solar wind's behavior is shaped by a complex interplay between plasma waves and instabilities at the sub-ion scale. This research provides valuable insights into the solar system's innermost regions and the origins of its turbulent plasma environment. Textiles exhibiting repeating patterns are susceptible to defects that affect their aesthetic appeal and functionality,  thereby reducing their value.  Identifying these defects in textiles is a complex challenge,  making defect detection and classification a pressing issue in the textile industry.  Most existing methods focus on traditional knit fabrics,  overlooking the growing market for textiles with patterned designs.  This paper introduces a novel approach to detecting defects in textiles with patterned designs by utilizing the properties of gabor gradients in oriented gradients (GHOG).  This proposed method surpasses previous performance benchmarks,  outperforming other methods in detecting defects in these types of fabrics.  Additionally,  we address the issue of defective textile data classification,  given the limited availability of data,  by employing a low-rank decomposition strategy.  This approach allows us to generate synthetic data from existing samples,  thus enhancing our training capabilities.  To validate the efficacy of our proposed method,  we created a comprehensive dataset consisting of 10 distinct textile patterns,  totaling 5000 images,  and varying levels of defects.  Our findings indicate that our method successfully identifies defects in these textures and demonstrates classification accuracy on our custom dataset.  Furthermore,  we successfully applied our proposed method to real-world textile defect classification scenarios.  This research has been publicly shared through https://github.com/TextileDefectECIT/TextileDefectClassification,  enabling others to access the code and dataset.  To evaluate our method's robustness,  we employed various metrics such as precision,  recall,  F1-score,  mean IU,  and mean pixel accuracy.  Our approach,  centered around ghog and low-rank decomposition,  yields superior results,  surpassing other state-of-the-art techniques.  Specifically,  our method achieves an mIU of 0.9537,  outperforming other methods,  and achieving an accuracy of 97.57%,  along with precision and recall of 0.9703 and 0.9537 respectively.  Notably,  our approach,  and associated code,  and custom dataset,  are publicly accessible through https://github.com/TextileDefectECIT/TextileDefectClassification.  This will facilitate other researchers in replicating our findings and potentially improving upon our method.  In terms of future work,  we envision extending our method to other domains,  and exploring other techniques that leverage low-rank and gabor gradients in oriented gradients (GHOG).

To effectively guide robotic visual navigation, a balance must be struck between exploration and exploitation.  While prior studies have primarily focused on regulating exploration, this research acknowledges that some degree of exploitation is also necessary to attain desired goals.  A novel information-theoretic approach is introduced to concurrently control exploration and exploitation within a single framework.  By leveraging the Shannnon information constraint in conjunction with a reward-based objective, this method enables robots to adaptively make the most of their surroundings and achieve their intended targets.  Experimental results from both simulated and real-world settings demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in creating a self-regulating navigation system.  Notably, this research marks the first instance where an autonomous robot successfully retrieves all objects in a complex environment without requiring any preconceived knowledge of its environment or object characteristics.  Moreover, when applied to a real robot, this research yields a navigation system that substantially surpasses existing benchmarks while also exhibiting user-like behavior.  A video showcasing the robot's navigation capabilities in real-world settings is available at https://youtu.be/6Q8xk6Q8xk6. As black holes and dark stars undergo mass changes, the rate of their mass loss is restricted according to the laws of general relativity. This study discovers a similar restriction applying to objects experiencing expansion in the environment of (possibly) Kerr black holes and dark holes, utilizing a method based on Bondi mass and incorporating the concept of acceleration in the Equivalence Principle. When the acceleration is minimal, the original restriction reverts to its initial form. Additionally, this work explores the connection to the Gravitational Wave LIGO/VIRGO collaboration's detection data, examining whether recently detected binary black hole mergers impose any limits on the acceleration, the outcome being negative. Finally, this work considers implications for string theory and membrane analogues, proposing modifications to their models to accommodate these restrictions. Lastly, future research possibilities are suggested. \textit{Note: This work was done while visiting the theoretical physics group at MIT, supported by sabbatical leave funding from University of Pittsburgh.} \end{document}

In modern smart grid implementations, numerous sensors embedded throughout the Power Distribution Network gather data that, when analyzed in real-time, can facilitate proactive incident response and enhance grid resilience. This research focuses on developing a method to detect incidents from sensor data streams by employing one-class classification techniques and real-time anomaly detection methods. Our results demonstrate that incorporating situational awareness and historical incident data into incident detection can optimize performance and accuracy, particularly in dynamic Power Distribution Networks. Additionally, we highlight key findings and suggest avenues for future research into integrating more advanced decision support systems into operational control centers. entity known as "metriques".

The $A$-matrix method effectively captures the spatially non-uniform behavior of topological insulators, as proven in previous studies. However, these studies assumed the presence of complete edge surfaces in the system's boundary. This paper relaxes that assumption, allowing for edge surfaces with holes by incorporating localized surface states, which can be generated by defects. Building on existing research, we show that the occurrence of chiral edge states in gapped, Hermitian systems is still indicative of a topological property, as demonstrated through examples in the rhombus and octagon shapes. Furthermore, we introduce a new topological property, which can be used to explain the presence of chiral edge states in these two systems, as well as extend the $A$-matrix approach to include dynamic systems by replacing the traditional Schrödinger equation with the Fokker-Planck equation. This allows us to study spatially non-uniform quantum systems and topological insulators subject to decoherence. By adapting the methods from previous studies, we find that decoherence can eliminate edge states only if the system's characteristic time is less than the decoherence time, otherwise the edge states will persist at a reduced intensity. Additionally, we show that the spatial distribution of states in topological insulators is resistant to decoherence and remains localized within a specific region. This research provides a new approach to studying topological insulators and their behavior under various conditions in both clean and decoherent environments. As a result, it may be possible to develop new materials with extended edge states by controlling their response to decoherence. Finally, we outline potential future research directions in this field. \end{abstract}

Browning and Sawin established that the number of non-zero trigonometric terms up to a given degree, which evaluate to a specific value modulo 1, is finite when defined over a specific field and satisfying certain conditions. We expand upon this by proving two additional results - one concerning the number of non-zero trigonometric terms over a specific type of field extension, which evaluate to a specific value modulo 1, and another concerning the number of non-Archimedean adics polynomials that evaluate to a specific value modulo the corresponding prime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these results hold without the requirement of a crucial technical assumption previously made by Browning and Sawin. We also show that these results can be applied to resolve two long-standing conjectures concerning the finiteness of certain arithmetic objects. Specifically, we resolve the finiteness of the Brahmagupta-Pell equations and the modular forms with specific properties, modulo their respective lattices. Additionally, we provide evidence for the broader conjecture put forth by Darmon and Rotger. We anticipate that our work will facilitate further research into the broader conjecture. The proof of our results relies on an innovative application of an earlier theorem concerning the dynamics of the 2x2 matrix matrix multiplication over finite fields, as well as key properties of polynomials with specific characteristics, which we have identified and analyzed. Furthermore, we have derived several additional results concerning the properties of such polynomials, which we believe will be of independent interest. We also utilize techniques from the theory of dynamical systems to derive upper limits for the size of certain sets of integers, which we have identified as relevant to our results. Finally, we have also applied techniques from the theory of adelic geometry to derive key estimates for the size of certain sets of integers, which arise from the evaluation of adelic forms over specific field extensions. We believe that our work will facilitate further research into the theory of adelic geometry. The adelic geometric analysis relied on the theory of moduli spaces of simultaneous torsions in abelian varieties, which we have analyzed using the techniques from the theory of geometric Galois representations. Achieving efficiency in training robotic manipulation skills involves transferring learned abilities from demonstration humans to autonomous robot operations. However, due to differences in the anatomy of human and robot hands, adapting these skills is challenging, particularly when handling objects with complex geometries. To overcome this problem, our research focuses on developing a new domain adaptation technique based on point cloud registration. This approach employs a novel method to align reference points from human demonstrations with the actual robotic setup, using tangent vectors and geodesic transport to account for 3D pose rotations and translations. Additionally, to enhance precision, our algorithm incorporates a manifold-based Iterative Closest Point (ICP) method that considers the specific geometry of the object and its impact on registration. Compared to traditional ICP, our results show significant improvements in alignment accuracy and a substantial reduction in computational time, with the potential to simplify the operability adaptation process. Successful applications of our technique have been demonstrated on various object manipulation tasks, including grasping, manipulation, and sorting operations. With its potential to automate tasks and bridge the gap between human and robotic operations, this method can contribute positively to areas like quality control and assembly. A video showcasing the method's effectiveness can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q6k6j8Q4Qo. The developed code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Robot-Learning-Sebastian/human2robot. Additionally, the results can be accessed on the GraspSim platform at https://graspim.com/. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. 2119698.
