This research introduces an advanced adaptive Gaussian-based correntropy-like measure for handling noisy graph signal recovery, taking into account the impact of kernel width on overall performance. We develop a strategy to automatically determine the optimal kernel width, enabling us to modify the loss function with it. By doing so, we convert the original problem into an efficient transversal filter operation, framed within a robust framework that incorporates data-driven incidence matrix adaptation and normalized node adaptive weighted least mean square (NWA-LSMS) methods. Our approach can be effectively applied to various real-world challenges, such as audio source separation and channel estimation. Our experimental findings demonstrate the proposed method's capability to achieve significant improvements over existing graph signal recovery methods, using either a fixed or optimizable kernel width, across multiple applications. For instance, in audio source separation, it managed to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio by 5.35 dB compared to the GS-2SM method. Additionally, it determined an optimal kernel width of 1.0473 for this particular scenario. Our source code is freely accessible at https://github.com/zheng-huang/SAGCSR. In this study, we demonstrate a precise estimate for the initial eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator subject to a Robin boundary condition, building upon previous work by G. Mondaini and H. Stoltzer concerning nonlinear Dirichlet problems. Our analysis involves proving that this eigenvalue ASlies upon combining the first Steklov eigenvalue of the same nonlinear elliptic operator with the square of the L^2 norm of the boundary data, all under the same minimax formulation. This result holds without any symmetry assumptions in the boundary data. We also extend this findings to more general nonlinear problems, including those involving potentials and smooth boundaries, and verify that these estimates remain precise even in the limiting case of domain degeneration. Moreover, our work includes a counterexample that illustrates the loss of variability in direction for Dirichlet boundary conditions, thereby differentiating this scenario from Robin boundary conditions under the same nonlinear curvature assumptions. A recently developed neural dependency parser utilizes a self-improving technique called auto-context, combining deep contextualized representations with an internal teacher to iteratively refine parsing accuracy. Although effective for parsers trained on abundant data, such methods prove challenging and expensive to execute on limited data sets. We introduce a modified strategy, deep contextualized auto-training, that replaces the internal teacher with an external mentor, yielding improved performance on parsing tasks within resource-constrained environments. We also develop a customized method for contextualized dependency parsers using the fastText tool, outperforming current state-of-the-art models on several benchmark datasets. Additionally, we create three new dependency parsing challenges to simulate real-world scenarios of varying data availability. We achieve successful results on these challenging datasets, including substantial improvements on a benchmark set for Arabic languages. A code repository for our work is available at https://github.com/DeepCAA/DeepCAA. DeepCAA has been added to the Hugging Face model hub at https://huggingface.co/DeepCAA. DeepCAA is also available as an open-source extension of spaCy at https://spacy.io/models/DeepCAA.

We investigated a specific class of graphs known as CFIM, which can be recognized in AT^2 time, and conducted two significant experiments to expand our understanding. Firstly, we demonstrated that the exclusive membership problem for CFIM graphs can be solved in O(n^5.1) time, providing a polynomial time solution for the first time. Furthermore, we proved that the graphs within this class are capable of being fully embodied within AC^0[p] structures, which have previously been shown to have a polynomial number of gates, thereby confirming a conjecture made by Beame and Natarajan in 2000. Secondly, we explored alternative recognition time complexities for CFIM graphs, particularly those with n, m, or d vertices or edges, and formulated several hypotheses based on our findings. Additionally, we established that certain dense and sparse graph classes can be recognized within the same time complexity as CFIM graphs, which led us to deduce that they too can be embodied within AC^0[p] structures with a polynomial number of gates. Building upon this, we proved a general theorem stating that any graph class capable of solving Boolean polynomial equations in AT^2 time can also be embodied within AC^0[p] structures with a polynomial number of gates. Finally, we used this theorem along with our earlier O(n^5.1) time solution to demonstrate that CFIM graphs can be recognized in O(n^5.1) time as well as within AC^0[p] structures with a polynomial number of gates. Lastly, we conducted an empirical analysis of our new recognition algorithm for CFIM graphs and observed through experiments that it outperforms the existing AT^2 algorithm in several instances while also offering improved density and sparsity recognitions. Notably, we observed that the new algorithm often achieves nearly linear time complexity in various scenarios. Moreover, we found through experiments that CFIM graphs can be embodied within AC^0[p] structures with a remarkably small number of gates. Specifically, our experiments showed that CFIM graphs can be effectively represented within AC^0[p] structures with as few as 6-7 gates. This finding not only affirms the conjecture made by Beame and Natarajan but also offers valuable insights into the underlying structures of CFIM graphs. In particular, when the atoms and cavity field initially become entangled in a particular manner, specifically in a Duan criterion violating state, it's discovered that this interaction results in consistent transmission of atom-emitted photons into the cavity, alongside the emergence of Rabi oscillations in both atoms' states. It's further established that this transmission remains unaffected by initial entanglement and that it can be described through a simple, intuitive physical explanation. Notably, when the atoms are moved apart, the Rabi oscillations in both atoms converge into a single, synchronized pattern. The study also investigates how entanglement is preserved and transmitted over longer distances, even in the absence of the cavity field. Crucially, when the cavity field is present but not entangled, it's found to not influence the transmission process. Instead, the focus shifts to the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, where one atom is coupled to the cavity field while the other is not, revealing distinct transmission patterns for each atom and highlighting the role of entanglement in the first atom with the cavity field in modifying these transmission patterns. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of entanglement's impact on single- and two-atom transmission behaviors in complex quantum systems. Based on these findings, it's possible that similar entanglement phenomena could be observed experimentally using modern technologies. The study also suggests potential applications for these non-intuitive quantum behaviors, particularly in the fields of quantum computing and cryptography. The research also offers potential avenues for further exploration into the transmission properties of complex, interacting quantum systems. The researchers behind the model recommend using ensemble methods with other deep learning models to further improve its accuracy. This research introduces HUMBI, a groundbreaking dataset featuring 3D human performance capture, comprising over 4.5 million animated characters captured through color and depth footage equivalent to 350 hours of video. The dataset leverages advanced multiview technology to track 3D human movements from 21 different viewpoints, resulting in precise 3D reconstructions. Building upon this framework, we present a novel evaluation challenge designed to test state-of-the-art 3D human animation techniques, focusing on tracking accuracy and efficiency. Our study compares the performance of various methods using HUMBI, with promising outcomes indicating that with sufficient training, characters can be reconstructed with near-perfect accuracy within a fraction of a second. Notably, our findings reveal that certain methods can achieve impressive tracking speeds of up to 60 frames per second on consumer-grade hardware. This research aims to drive innovation in 3D human animation capture, with potential applications spanning computer-generated animation, video game design, and content creation for virtual reality and augmented reality platforms. In artificial intelligence, using reinforcement learning to learn policies across multiple tasks is an area of active research. Although theory suggests this approach prevents overfitting and improves learning efficiency, practical applications often experience negative effects like slow convergence and decreased performance. We discovered that these issues arise from reinforcement learning methods that train a single skill module, causing policies to intersect destructively, especially in tasks that require more complex behaviors. To overcome this challenge, we developed a method that trains separate modules for distinct actions, allowing them to operate independently and significantly improve performance in challenging scenarios. Our findings are supported by over 30 synthetic and real-world experiments. Additionally, we created an interactive online demo that showcases our solution's capabilities. This can be accessed at https://mlquad.uni-bonn.de/multitask-rl/. A detailed description of the system's architecture and source code is available at https://github.com/Uni-Bonn-MLQuad/modular-rl. This project has been validated through collaboration with industry partners and published in a leading journal. Typically, the performance of small-scale heat engines is evaluated using the maximum efficiency theory developed by Carnot. To explore the potential for higher average work output from these systems, we're examining ideal finite-duration heat engines with both fully controllable and restricted control mechanisms. To this end, we've developed a general mathematical framework that allows us to derive analytical formulas for the maximum average work capabilities of these systems in terms of their thermal contact times and the number of controllable variables. Notably, our results indicate that engines with limited control over their internal processes can outperform those with complete control, particularly at shorter thermal contact times. To validate the practical relevance of our findings, we've also developed a method for numerically estimating the average work capabilities of quasi-static finite-duration heat engines. To illustrate the generality of our approach, we've applied our methods to both a classical point-particle system and a quantum Tunnel-Raman system. Historically, severe hurricanes and storm surges have posed significant threats to the energy sector in the United States, resulting in substantial financial losses and disruptions to energy production and distribution. To minimize these impacts, utility companies and energy managers must develop advanced strategies for predicting and mitigating the effects of severe weather events. Building on previous research that focused on the spatial impact of hurricanes, this study aims to expand our understanding by investigating the temporal and spatial dynamics of storm surges on both natural gas systems and power transmission lines. By utilizing a combination of geographic information systems and analytical methods, we evaluated the extent of storm surge-related damage to both types of infrastructure, identifying specific locations and levels of damage along with the distance storm surges traversed from the coast. Our results indicate that both natural gas systems and power transmission lines are susceptible to significant disruptions during severe weather events, with the extent of damage varying by location, distance from the coast, and level of storm surge intensity. By sharing our findings with energy stakeholders and utility companies, we hope to inform their decision-making and risk management tactics to better prepare for future storm surges, reducing the likelihood and severity of energy service disruptions. With ongoing climate change, the likelihood and impact of severe weather events like hurricanes and storm surges will only grow, underscoring the importance of proactive planning and preparedness measures to safeguard energy systems and prevent widespread disruptions. Given the broad applicability of our research, our approach can be adapted to assess the effects of severe weather events on other critical infrastructure systems, such as transportation and communication networks. By analyzing this system, we identify two types of invariant measures - those following the SRB hypothesis and non-absolutely continuous measures. Although the non-absolutely continuous measures have higher entropy than those following the SRB hypothesis, we observe that the system does not converge to these higher entropy measures, raising questions about the validity of entropy approachability in this case. Additionally, we find that non-absolutely continuous measures can be represented through the Arnold-Wender theorem, revealing a connection between the heterochaos map and the Dyck system. Furthermore, our study resolves a challenge posed by Wender in [20], concerning the identification of maximal entropy measures for the Dyck system. We also provide numerical support for our findings through various statistical tests and confirm the non-approachability of the most entropy-rich measures, under both uniform and Lebesgue measure initial conditions, using multiple evaluation methods - false nearest neighbors, nearest neighbor density, regression, and Monte Carlo integration - with the help of our novel Heterochaos baker map algorithm. To achieve this, we propose a novel framework that extracts a style from paired images and applies it uniformly across entire images. Unlike previous methods, our technique can apply a learned style extracted from training data to images outside of the training dataset. Both forward (high to low) and reverse (low to high) tone mapping operations are supported, and we enhance the output of a standard image enhancement model to produce more visually appealing results. Evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, specifically in dealing with reverse tone mapping and producing high-quality outputs from images outside of the training dataset. Our code and dataset are publicly available for review.

Artificial intelligence inspired by the brain's active learning process is gaining momentum in developing adaptive and efficient agents. This study introduces a highly engaged active inference approach for independent robot navigation. Unlike static environments commonly used in robotics research, our method effectively handles dynamic and unpredictable surroundings, in which the robot receives sporadic sensory inputs and uncertain global information. We demonstrate that a robot employing this method can proactively control its perception, strike a balance between exploration and exploitation, and maintain a precise understanding of its surroundings, ultimately leading to optimal navigation. The research highlights a fundamental similarity between active inference and the intrinsic motivation concept, and showcases a feasible and practical approach for the creation of autonomous and self-motivated robotic agents. To overcome this issue, a novel data compression technique utilizing a dual convolutional autoencoder is proposed, where the original data and its two-dimensional projection are used as inputs to the autoencoder to leverage their inherent information effectively. With a weight-pruning strategy after the autoencoder's training, the model can achieve significant sparsity and reduce its complexity, resulting in a viable method for large-scale event data compression. When applied to simulated minimum-branching fraction LHCb data, a 7.5-fold compression ratio is achieved with only a 0.03% average bitrate increase compared to the original data. Moreover, this approach exhibits promising low latency, with a compression-decompression latency of 2.5 ms for 5000 events. Furthermore, the framework's framework event-oriented design allows for the deployment of a hybrid compression strategy combining this approach with existing compression techniques to achieve an overall 5.6-fold compression ratio. Additionally, the model's compactness enables it to be deployed on FPGAs efficiently, where even with severe on-chip bandwidth constraints, a 4.5-fold compression ratio can be achieved with only a 0.04% average bitrate increase. A convex geometric hypergraph is a type of hypergraph that exhibits geometric properties, where its vertices and edges are part of a specific convex shape. We investigate a problem involving the saturation number of a 3-realiseable geometric hypergraph, which represents the minimum number of additional edges a substructure must acquire to ensure it cannot be 3-realiseable. Our analysis involves establishing a lower limit for this substructure through a more general theorem applicable to any geometric hypergraph, involving the concept of minimal edges and a specific area calculation within a convex shape. We further demonstrate challenges in calculating exact saturation numbers and instead provide asymptotic approximations for certain geometric hypergraphs. Additionally, we define the concept of geometric Piperones and demonstrate a connection between these and a known problem in number theory to gain insight into the values of certain saturation numbers. Lastly, we provide a method to establish a lower limit for the saturation number of any geometric hypergraph that is 3-realiseable when restricted to edges within a specific size. This work is based on a recent study by Fiala et al. and is part of ongoing research in this field. All visualisations used in this paper were created using GeoGebra. A new method for robot climbing has been created using data collected from Pacific eels, which enables robots to move efficiently on varied surfaces by mimicking the unique gait pattern of these animals. By taking into account several key factors that influence the eels' movements, such as their body composition and the texture of their surroundings, this method makes it possible for robots to travel at high speeds, even on challenging surfaces like those found in household environments. To test its effectiveness, several robots have been built using different manufacturing approaches and their performance has been evaluated in controlled experiments, which included scaling the eels' movements to fit different sizes. The results show that this method allows for robust and adaptive movement on various surfaces and even predicts when robots are likely to fail on certain textures. With further advancements, this technology has the potential to be used in a range of applications, including search and rescue operations, where robots may need to navigate difficult-to-reach areas. This research proposes a novel framework to design the most effective cancer treatment strategies, taking into account the unique characteristics of each patient and the intricate interactions between the disease and its treatment. A dynamic model of a patient's condition is developed by combining a stochastic process governing the colon-cancer induced immune reaction, which is modeled as a nonlinear system with random parameters. To identify the optimal treatment, the model is optimized through a customized approach, which is challenged as an open-issue problem, requiring the estimation of model parameters, the definition of optimal treatments, and the maximization of patients' survival rates. By applying the Fokker-Planck equation and a stochastic maximum principle, two different control laws are designed, which are then validated by solving the resulting nonlinear partial differential equations numerically. The proposed framework is successfully tested on simulated colon-cancer induced immune reaction data. Furthermore, the study highlights the significance of considering both patient variability and treatment options in the design of cancer treatment strategies. Additionally, the research underscores the importance of incorporating colon-cancer induced immune reactions in treatment design. While this study focuses on colon-cancer induced immune reactions, the proposed framework can be applied to modeling other types of cancer and their interactions with the immune system. From a practical perspective, the framework can assist oncologists in developing individualized treatment plans, taking into account patient diversity and treatment options. Ultimately, this leads to improved patients' outcomes and quality of life. Several potential applications and extensions of this research are discussed. One such area is the integration of the proposed framework with existing clinical decision support systems to enhance their decision-making capabilities. Another possible direction is the incorporation of the colon-cancer induced immune reaction model into existing epidemiological models to gain a deeper understanding of the disease's dynamics. Additionally, this model can be utilized to investigate the causal relationship between colon-cancer induced immune reactions and other types of cancer. Furthermore, this research can contribute to the development of methods for validating colon-cancer induced immune reaction models through the analysis of patients' medical images. Lastly, this study can facilitate the exploration of new approaches for modeling and controlling colon-cancer induced immune reactions. In summary, this research provides a novel framework for individualized cancer treatment, taking into account the unique characteristics of each patient and the intricate interactions between the disease and its treatment. This framework can be applied to model various types of cancer and their interactions with the immune system, leading to improved patients' outcomes and quality of life. Additionally, this research can contribute to the advancement of methods for validating disease models through data analysis and imaging

The growing demand for mobile data is driving mobile network service providers to upgrade their systems by incorporating Device-to-Device (D2D) technology, which enables direct device communication without passing through the base station. As a result, these networks can offer improved network capacity, reduced traffic at base stations, and increased available spectrum frequency. To effectively utilize D2D communication, scheduling algorithms are necessary to manage the selection of operating frequencies, time slots, and data transmission areas. Since traditional scheduling methods based on centralized algorithms and channel access control have limitations, a new method based on frequency aggragation and random access has been introduced. However, this new approach requires addressing the challenges of managing interference and availability of available resources, particularly in urban areas. To tackle these challenges, we propose a real-time scheduling algorithm that learns from real-time data and make decisions accordingly. Our approach, which is an application of the Advanced Long Short-Term Memory (ALSTM) deep learning method, successfully learns the patterns of D2D communication and other data transmissions, and uses this knowledge to effectively schedule D2D transmissions. Our simulation results show that our proposed algorithm achieves significant improvements in overall network capacity and fairness compared to traditional algorithms. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of using deep learning methods in real-time scheduling for D2D networks and predict that future wireless networks will be largely based on this technology. Finally, we outline the potential challenges and limitations of implementing this technology in practical settings.

This paper investigates the problem of identifying incidents on evolving networks, a crucial application for traffic surveillance systems. To tackle this challenge, we have developed a two-part framework consisting of incident detection and identification methods. Firstly, our dynamic network anomaly detection algorithm using the Autoencoder and k-nearest neighbors (DAKNN) effectively recognizes incidents by analyzing temporal graph sequences at predefined road junctions. It employs an autoencoder to encode network structures and compares the reconstructed graphs with the current one using k-nearest neighbors' similarity ratios. If the ratio falls below a predetermined threshold, an incident is detected. Subsequently, to associate detected incidents with specific road segments, we utilize the minimum spanning tree of spatial relationships between nodes. By mapping temporal graph sequences and matching them with spanning tree segments, incident occurrences are precisely identified. Numerical experiments conducted on real-world road networks demonstrate the capability of our framework to accurately recognize incidents compared to traditional methods. Additionally, this approach offers the added benefit of enabling incident duration tracking. To validate our framework's robustness, experiments were performed with varying parameter settings, including different incident frequencies and graph encoding methods. Furthermore, results show that this algorithm can effectively identify incidents even when faced with limited observation periods. To address this capability, we propose an incident identification method utilizing pre-incident graph information. This approach involves mapping pre-incident graphs with observed graphs and matching them to detect incidents. These experiments demonstrate the capability of our framework to provide accurate incident recognition and identification in real-time. To assess our approach, we compared its performance with traditional methods using the F-score metric. Results show that our framework outperforms these methods with higher F-scores and reduced false detection rates. Our dataset showcases its usefulness through experiments conducted on deep learning classification tasks, revealing that even basic models can achieve high levels of accuracy in identifying and assessing colorectal polyp histopathology. The UniToPatho dataset is accessible at https://bit.ly/unito-patho, allowing researchers to build upon our findings and contribute to the advancement of this field. Furthermore, we have initiated a data challenge to stimulate research in this domain, with more details available at https://bit.ly/unito-patho-challenge. To ensure the integrity of our dataset, we have made public our training and testing protocols, data preprocessing methods, and model implementations at https://github.com/unito-patho/UnitoPatho. Our ultimate goal is to enable the development of an automated system that can supplement the diagnostic capabilities of human pathologists, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes. To this end, we envision a system that can rapidly review numerous samples, providing accurate and consistent diagnoses that can be leveraged for statistical analyses and clinical decision-making purposes. By automating the colorectal polyps classification and adenoma dysplasia evaluation processes, we anticipate significant reductions in the time and resources required for histopathological examinations, ultimately benefiting both patients and the healthcare system as a whole. With the UniToPatho dataset serving as a cornerstone, we are confident that substantial breakthroughs can be achieved in the field of histopathological analysis, ultimately paving the way for the widespread adoption of automated diagnostic systems in clinical practice. This research explores the issue of data leakage in zero-error source encoding through a graph-theoretic perspective. Initially, we establish the formal concept of data leakage tolerance (DLT) for a set of sources and develop two primary methods for determining the DLT. Firstly, we outline an approach to directly calculate the DLT via a source's conditional entropy distribution (SED) and specific graph connectivity properties. Alternatively, we propose a dual method that applies linear programming to find the maximum DLT. Additionally, we provide a framework for combining individual DLTs in cases of composite sources. Our study further examines how data leakage influences information release problems from an information-theoretic standpoint, revealing instances where source encoding with restricted data leakage yields more informative outcomes than unrestricted encoding. Finally, we investigate the relationship between data leakage and source type, observing that Gaussian sources generally exhibit more robust data leakage than sources with discrete outputs. Our research offers a theoretical foundation and methodological tools for managing data leakage in zero-error source encoding applications. These findings are expected to contribute to the development of guidelines for responsibly releasing and encoding sensitive data while maintaining specified levels of leakage tolerance. Lastly, our study also sheds light on the intricate interplay between data leakage and information release problems within information theory. Deep learning solutions have been widely accepted as the most effective approach to resolving the issue of limited pixels in Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images, which causes poor image quality in remote sensing applications.  However, existing deep learning models are often tested on optical or other types of remote sensing images, not SAR images, due to the distinct characteristics and complexities of SAR imaging.  This research presents a new model, called MrSARP, which is designed to address the challenges of SAR image super-resolution through a well-organized database of paired images and a novel neural network architecture that incorporates a multi-scale hierarchical structure.  The results show that MrSARP outperforms other leading models in the field by achieving a significant improvement of 8.47 dB in the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and 15.91% in the equivalent number of looks (ENL) on the relevant remote sensing image quality metric.  Furthermore, MrSARP demonstrates its ability to effectively handle compressed SAR images by achieving a notable enhancement of 6.13 dB in the PSNR and 10.08% in the ENL on the relevant remote sensing image quality metric.  The proposed model, MrSARP, is now available as open-source software for other researchers to use. One of the most successful methods for approximately solving difficult combinatorial optimization problems using quantum computers is the Quantum Alternating Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). However, the challenge lies in determining the optimal hybrid parameters that balance quantum and classical optimization techniques. We propose a novel approach called Bayesian Maximization (BM) that deterministically selects effective hybrid parameters for QAOA without relying on time-consuming surrogate-based assessments. BM leverages machine learning and accurate cost estimates from nested surrogate models within the Maximum Probabilistic Path Search (MPPS) framework to choose its parameters. Compared to existing methods, BM results in significantly higher success rates in finding the exact solution for a defined problem and outperforms QAOA-VQE in most cases, especially for larger problem sizes. BM also offers the advantage of reducing circuit depth by approximately 50%, making it more suitable for near-term quantum computers. BM's performance can be further enhanced by taking into account problem-specific structure using a variant called Structural Bayesian Maximization (SBM). SBM's efficiency is demonstrated by a reduction in circuit depth of up to 85% and an improvement in success rates of up to one order of magnitude for a defined problem. SBM's performance comes at the cost of increased classical processing time for some problems, but not all, so it is essential to choose the problems for which SBM is beneficial. We establish that a birational transformation between two smooth varieties preserves their quantum toric noncommutative topology, maintaining key properties including $\mathbb{C}$-algebra isomorphism, functorial equivalence, and consistent smoothness. Furthermore, this transformation also preserves instanton invariants and $gl_2$-quantum cohomology across all stages of the Mukai-Umeda filtration. Additionally, our findings can be extended to include NCD's toric completion, and we provide supporting examples that illustrate the importance of working within the broader class of quantum toric NCD's, rather than solely relying on Hodge theoretic approaches. Lastly, we conjecture that relative quantum topology should exhibit a deeper connection with CM pairs, and speculate that it should remain invariant under certain types of birational transformations beyond those that are merely rational.

This paper challenges the conventional view of the Scientific Revolution as a seamless merger of science and philosophy.  Instead, it contends that science and philosophy became distinct pursuits at that time.  The paper also investigates Galileo's stance on this separation, concluding that he held a dual role in both fields and exemplified the shift towards a scientific worldview that prioritizes empirical evidence and instrumental reasoning over speculative philosophy.  This analysis positions Galileo as a bridge between the philosophical and scientific traditions of his time, rather than a pioneer of scientific empiricism.  Furthermore, the paper offers an alternative explanation for Galileo's famous conflict with the Church, suggesting that his scientific methods were not the primary cause of the controversy, but rather his earlier critiques of Aristotelian philosophy, which had implications for theology.  This narrative underscores the complexities of the Scientific Revolution and highlights the pivotal role Galileo played in the evolution of science and the separation of the two disciplines.  Ultimately, the paper contends that his legacy serves as a reminder of the perils of scientific hubris and the importance of humility in the pursuit of knowledge.

We introduce Scribe, a novel technique combining interactive transformations and template synthesis to streamline task-oriented training for programming.
